title: Enhanced laser-driven ion acceleration through electromagnetic energy coupling in annular sector targets
Experimental tuning of electron energy gain via laser focus shift in a laser-driven plasma wakefield accelerator
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a combined experimental and simulation study on electron acceleration in a laser-driven plasma wakefield accelerator utilizing the plasma telescope mechanism. By employing a 15-J laser with its focal spot smaller than the matching condition, and systematically tuning the laser focus position relative to the gas cell entrance, we generate an electron beam with energy of up to 1.4 GeV when the laser is focused a few millimeters upstream of the plasma entrance. We further observe that electron self-injection and subsequent acceleration occur only when the laser is focused within 2.2 mm upstream to 2.4 mm downstream of the gas-cell entrance. Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations reproduce the experimental observations and predict a maximum electron energy of 2.2 GeV at the optimal focal position. Both the experiments and simulations reveal a clear injection threshold when the laser focus is placed too far upstream of the plasma entrance. In this case, excessive laser diffraction prevents efficient refocusing by the plasma telescope, thereby suppressing wakefield injection and acceleration. These results provide experimental evidence that the plasma telescope mechanism can support the generation of GeV-scale electron beams in laser wakefield accelerators. Furthermore, they identify the laser focal position on the plasma density up-ramp as a critical parameter governing electron injection and energy gain, offering important guidance for the optimization of future plasma-telescope-based acceleration schemes.</jats:p>

title: Issue Information: Plasma Process. Polym. 12/2026
Fluorescence polarization patterns by spatial shaping with interfering laser pulse components
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report on polarization patterns generated by spatial laser beam shaping applied on two-photon excited fluorescence of a dye. For this purpose, a focused spatially modulated laser beam component is overlapped with an unfocused Gaussian beam component in common path configuration and the induced fluorescence is recorded polarization dependent. This allows for producing desired spatial polarization light fields and leads to polarization selective fluorescence intensity patterns which can well be visualized. The devised spatial polarization shaping method is prospective for optical and biophotonic imaging applications.</jats:p>

title: Advanced Surface Coatings for Biosensors: A Review of Atmospheric Plasma Innovations
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biosensing relies on the precise engineering of the bio‐interface to achieve good performance (e.g., sensitivity, working range, stability) in complex samples. Despite their favorable properties, metals, polymers, carbon nanotubes, and paper remain challenging biosensing substrates due to surface inertness, biofouling, and poor biomolecule adhesion. Wet‐chemical modification can address these limitations but is frequently hindered by multi‐step protocols, chemical waste, and substrate‐specific constraints. This review demonstrates plasma as a versatile, more sustainable, and dry‐state alternative for the advanced (bio)functionalization of biosensor surfaces. Atmospheric plasma is discussed as a universal toolkit for creating high‐performance interfaces, including bioreceptor immobilization, engineered roughness, anti‐biofouling layers, and stabilization for shelf‐life by depositing tailored ultra‐thin films to enhance biosensor performance, essential for the next generation of biosensors.</jats:p>

title: Mixed-Precision GPU Acceleration for Large-Scale Minimum Enclosing Ball Problems
items.abstract: <jats:p>A mixed-precision GPU-oriented optimization framework is developed for computing the minimum enclosing ball of a collection of balls. The approach is built on an equivalent second-order cone programming reformulation and a relative-type inexact proximal augmented Lagrangian method (ripALM), which provides a high-accuracy optimization backbone while solving the inner subproblems only to a progress-dependent relative accuracy. The proximal augmented Lagrangian inherits a constraint-wise separable structure: its objective, gradient, generalized Hessian, and multiplier updates can be efficiently evaluated on GPUs as parallel maps over the input balls followed by reductions. To further improve efficiency, a mixed-precision reduction strategy is introduced. A low-precision ripALM run identifies balls near the approximate boundary, a high-precision ripALM run refines the reduced problem, and a full a posteriori feasibility check detects and reintroduces any violated discarded balls. Thus, low precision is used only for screening and warm starting, while the final feasibility is enforced against the original problem. Experiments on synthetic and real-data instances show that the proposed methods can compute accurate solutions, with GPU execution providing substantial speedups and mixed-precision reduction further reducing running times on most tested instances.</jats:p>

title: Observational Constraints on Granda–Oliveros and Interacting Holographic Dark Energy in Light of DESI DR2 Observations: Implications for Cosmic Acceleration
items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent observational data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) and Type Ia supernovae compilations provide unprecedented precision on late-time cosmic expansion, offering a critical test for dynamical alternatives to the cosmological constant (ΛCDM). In this paper, we present a comprehensive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) observational constraint and diagnostic evaluation of two prominent holographic dark energy (HDE) frameworks: Granda–Oliveros Holographic Dark Energy (GO-HDE), featuring a derivative-dependent infrared cutoff (ρGO=3MP2(αH2+βH˙)), and Interacting Holographic Dark Energy (IHDE), incorporating a non-gravitational dark sector energy exchange (Q=3bH(ρm+ρDE)). We constrain both models using cosmic-chronometer measurements, Type Ia supernova distance moduli from the Pantheon compilation, and baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from DESI DR2. For GO-HDE, we obtain α=0.967−0.037+0.041 and β=0.685−0.048+0.052, while the IHDE model yields cpar=0.717−0.046+0.051 and an interaction coupling b=0.0225−0.0085+0.0082. All constraints quoted in this abstract are conditional on the adopted diagonal-covariance approximation, the Gaussian prior on Ωm0 and the fixed sound horizon rd. Although the baseline IHDE analysis indicates a nominal 2.7σ preference for a non-zero interaction, this preference disappears when the Gaussian matter-density prior is replaced by a broad flat prior, for which b=0.0184−0.0495+0.0452, which is consistent with zero. We further identify an intrinsic background degeneracy in GO-HDE, demonstrating that the apparent precision of its cutoff parameters is partly inherited from the adopted prior. Separate analyses of the observational probes reveal no statistically significant overall dataset tension in either model, under the diagonal-covariance approximation adopted here, with Δχtens2=5.61 for GO-HDE and 4.77 for IHDE, each for seven degrees of freedom. Both scenarios reproduce the transition from decelerated to accelerated expansion, with ztrans=0.673−0.020+0.025 for GO-HDE and ztrans=0.627−0.022+0.023 for IHDE. We also examine the evolution of the adiabatic sound speed and the high-redshift behaviour of the GO-HDE energy density. The adiabatic sound speed is negative at the GO-HDE posterior median, while the IHDE result exhibits a pole near z≃0.27. Since the adiabatic sound speed is not generally identical to the rest-frame sound speed, these findings motivate a dedicated perturbation analysis but do not, by themselves, establish a physical instability. At the posterior median, the GO-HDE dark-energy density changes sign near z≃2.26 and is therefore negative at the DESI Lyman-α redshift z=2.33; this redshift is prior-dependent, and the negative density means the model cannot be read as a positive holographic energy density at high redshift. Overall, our results show that both models can describe the observed background expansion, while their inferred parameter constraints remain sensitive to prior assumptions and modelling choices. The phenomenological status of the GO cutoff and the absence of a large-scale-structure analysis remain important limitations of the present study.</jats:p>

title: SPS/MPS–Cl− Synergistic Acceleration in TSV Copper Electroplating: A Proposed Interfacial Activation and Cu+-Reservoir Cycle and Its Experimental Basis
items.abstract: <jats:p>The filling of blind through-silicon vias (TSVs) by copper electrodeposition depends on how halide ions and sulfur-bearing accelerators act together at the electrode–electrolyte interface. This work examines the SPS/MPS–Cl− system by combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of adsorption on Cu(111), B3LYP frontier-orbital calculations, chronoamperometry (CA) with stepwise chloride injection, CuCl(s) dissolution experiments, and four comparative filling tests in 20 × 60 μm vias. Three observations are established directly by experiment: (i) with no chloride added, SPS and MPS both suppress copper deposition, lowering the steady-state current at an applied potential of −0.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl by 4.31 and 4.76 mA; (ii) subsequent chloride injection reverses the inhibition within seconds and raises the current by 11.12 mA (SPS) and 6.10 mA (MPS); and (iii) SPS and MPS both convert insoluble CuCl(s) into soluble species in aqueous suspension, the SPS system dissolving the precipitate far more completely and giving a much larger cathodic response. Guided by these results, by the MD/DFT calculations and by the previous literature, we propose an eight-step interfacial cycle in which chloride triggers S–S cleavage of adsorbed SPS, MPS–Cu(I)–Cl and Cl–Cu(I)–SPS–Cu(I)–Cl act as a slow-release and a direct-reduction Cu(I) reservoir, and SPS is regenerated through Cu(II)-driven oxidative coupling accompanied by CuCl(s) precipitation. The cycle keeps the macroscopic framework of the curvature-enhanced accelerator coverage (CEAC) model and adds the Cu(I) complexation chemistry that the model omits. In the vias, the same chemistry accelerates deposition preferentially at the opening and closes the feature prematurely, which shows that chloride-triggered acceleration is necessary but not sufficient for bottom-up filling and must be balanced by a suppressor and a leveler. The evidence behind every step is graded explicitly: the six-membered-ring intermediate and the dinuclear Cu(I) complex remain hypotheses that require in situ molecular-scale verification.</jats:p>

title: Advances in adiabatic rotational and vibrational raman excitation of molecular hydrogen
Frequency-tuned impedance matching for pulsed capacitively coupled plasmas: analysis of self-consistent circuit-plasma coupling
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Pulsed capacitively coupled plasmas (CCPs) exhibit strongly time-dependent electrical characteristics because the plasma density, sheath structure, and plasma conductivity change as a function of time within each pulse period. This makes impedance matching difficult when the driving frequency and matching-network elements are fixed. In this work, a self-consistent circuit-plasma simulation model is used to investigate frequency-tuned impedance matching for pulsed CCPs. The model couples an implicit PIC/MCC plasma kinetic simulation with an external RF circuit including a generator, matching network, and reactor stray branch. The plasma impedance is extracted from the simulated CCP voltage and current waveforms using Fourier analysis. Under fixed-frequency operation at
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mn>13.56</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mtext> </mml:mtext>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>MHz</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , the reflection coefficient magnitude remains high during the effective pulse-on phase and a pronounced reflected-power peak appears after pulse ignition. A frequency-tuned matching strategy is then developed by determining, from the time-dependent plasma impedance, the driving frequency that minimizes the reflection coefficient magnitude while the matching-network elements remain fixed. The results show that frequency tuning strongly suppresses the reflected power during the pulse-on phase, while the power absorbed by the plasma changes only weakly under the imposed constant-generator-output-power condition. The results provide a proof-of-principle demonstration that driving-frequency modulation can compensate for transient impedance variations, reduce the reflected-power burden, and improve matching efficiency in pulsed CCPs without changing the matching-network elements within the pulse.
                  </jats:p>

title: Study of the ionization in air-breathing electric rockets with VLEO atmospheric propellants and typical laboratory mixtures
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This work investigates the ionization of atmospheric propellant in air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP) systems for satellites operating in Very-Low Earth Orbit (VLEO). Plasma formation inside the ionization chamber of an air-breathing thruster is studied to gain insights on physical phenomena involved in ABEP technology. A time-dependent zero-dimensional model of the plasma chamber is formulated, that accounts for a comprehensive set of reactions for nitrogen, oxygen and argon. This model is implemented within a numerical framework to simulate plasma ignition at different operating parameters defined to describe geometry, intake behaviour, input power, magnetic field interactions, acceleration mechanism, and VLEO environmental conditions. The simulation results include the evolution in time of plasma density, composition and reaction rates during the ignition transient until stationary conditions. The study identifies the plasma ignition envelope by analysing the dependencies of plasma properties on mass flow rate, electron temperature, and ions-to-neutrals residence times ratio. The composition and density of the plasma are characterized across different regimes, revealing a transition between molecular and atomic ions dominance. NO

title: Plasma Cell Leukemia: Aggressive Disease Hidden in Plasma Cell Biology
items.abstract: <jats:p>Plasma cell leukemia (PCL) represents the most aggressive manifestation of plasma cell neoplasia. Despite sharing a common cellular origin and numerous molecular features with multiple myeloma (MM), PCL exhibits a strikingly different biological behavior that is characterized by the ability of malignant plasma cells to escape the bone-marrow niche, survive in circulation, and disseminate to extramedullary sites. Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying this transition may provide important insights into the aggressive nature of the disease. This review focuses on alterations occurring within malignant plasma cells and examines how they distinguish leukemic plasma cells from their counterparts in conventional multiple myeloma. Particular attention is given to their changes in cellular adhesion and homing, interactions with the bone-marrow microenvironment, proliferative activity, apoptotic regulation, and cellular adaptation to survival outside the protective marrow niche. By integrating genomic, transcriptomic, immunophenotypic, and microenvironmental findings, we explore the biological similarities and differences between PCL and conventional MM. Furthermore, we discuss how advances in molecular characterization have influenced prognostic risk stratification and the development of biologically directed therapeutic strategies, including targeted agents and T-cell-redirecting immunotherapies. Connecting these biological insights with emerging clinical evidence may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of PCL and support the development of more effective, disease-specific therapeutic approaches.</jats:p>

title: An Efficient SBR Ray-Tracing Implementation for Urban Propagation Modeling Using LBVH Acceleration
items.abstract: <jats:p>Repeated shooting-and-bouncing-ray (SBR) simulations in urban environments involve numerous ray–scene intersection queries, resulting in substantial computational cost. This paper presents an engineering implementation that combines an extended-Morton-code (EMC)-based linear bounding volume hierarchy (LBVH) with ray classification to accelerate SBR-based urban radio-propagation prediction. The static scene is hierarchically organized, and candidate-node lists are generated for spatial–directional shafts, allowing rays associated with different transmitter–receiver configurations to access relevant LBVH subtrees without repeating classification. The proposed implementation reduces ray-traversal and intersection-testing time, while predicted propagation paths and electromagnetic parameters agree closely with Wireless InSite results.</jats:p>

title: Combined laser irradiation effects at the cutaneous infl ammatory response during tattoo pigment removal (an experimental study)
items.abstract: <jats:p>The authors present results of an experimental study with Wistar rats on the effectiveness of combined laser irradiation at wavelengths 532 nm and 1064 nm for tattoo pigment removal. The aim of this study was to assess morphological changes in the skin and depth of laser light penetration exposure in the discussed combined modality compared to monochromatic irradiation. In the control groups, patients were treated separately with laser wavelengths 532 nm and 1064 nm, while in the experimental group both wavelengths were applied consequently. Histological examination revealed that the combined method gives the deepest penetration (120-150 μm) and nearly complete destruction of pigment in both superficial and deep dermal layers, though it causes a pronounced inflammatory reaction. Monochromatic 532 nm irradiation showed superficial effects (40-70 μm) with pigment retention in deep layers and epidermal atrophy, whereas 1064 nm irradiation demonstrated intermediate penetration depth (80-110 μm) with uniform pigment destruction and minimal damage to surrounding tissues. These findings confirm that the choice of laser therapy should be based on the depth of pigment location and clinical objectives. The combined approach is optimal for complete pigment removal, while monochromatic 1064 nm irradiation may be recommended for cases requiring minimal damage to superficial skin layers.</jats:p>

title: Nonlinear dynamics of dual acoustic waves in dusty plasmas on the lunar shady-side
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Weakly nonlinear electrostatic waves are examined in a dusty-plasma model for the lunar nightside wake during the Moon’s passage through the Earth’s magnetotail. The linear spectrum contains a fast dust-ion-acoustic wave (DIAW), governed mainly by ion inertia, and a slow dust-acoustic wave (DAW), governed by dust inertia. A Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) reduction shows that the DAW remains rarefactive over the considered electron-depletion and temperature-ratio ranges, whereas the DIAW crosses a polarity-reversal boundary, where the quadratic nonlinearity vanishes. This boundary marks the limit of the KdV ordering rather than a physical amplitude singularity. Retaining cubic nonlinearity gives a Gardner description of the near-critical DIAW. Within the adopted lunar-wake parameter domain, the critical line remains in the positive-cubic-coefficient region, so the model admits polarity-selective Gardner solitons and the dual-polarity modified Korteweg–de Vries (mKdV) limit but does not reach the flat-top Gardner limiting sequence. The results identify how the two acoustic branches differ in nonlinear polarity and in the accessibility of near-critical electrostatic structures in this lunar-wake model.</jats:p>

title: Two‐Step Tapering‐Collapse Method Enables Element‐Interdiffused Cladding for Enhanced Laser Amplification in Yb:YAG Single Crystal Fibers
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The development of high‐power single‐crystal fiber (SCF) lasers is critically hindered by the lack of a reliable cladding scheme to confine the optical mode and ensure beam quality. Here, we propose and demonstrate a two‐step tapering‐collapse method for the first time to fabricate a high‐quality cladding on Yb:YAG SCFs based on elemental interdiffusion. This in‐situ formed transition layer with graded elemental composition effectively reduces the abrupt structural and thermomechanical discontinuities at the interface between the core and cladding. Consequently, the numerical aperture of the SCF is significantly reduced from 0.280 to 0.199. In a master oscillator power amplifier configuration, the clad SCF delivers a remarkable 52.1% enhancement in slope efficiency compared to its bare counterpart, accompanied by a substantially improved near‐field beam profile. This work establishes a facile and effective route to high‐performance clad SCFs, offering a promising path to unlock their potential as gain media for next‐generation lasers.</jats:p>

title: Hypolipidemic effects of laser therapy and kinesiotherapy in lipid metabolic disorders (a 3-month follow-up)
items.abstract: <jats:p>In recent years, significant progress has been achieved in  pharmacotherapy (PT) of lipid metabolism disorders (LMD) in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD). In most cases, pharmacotherapy produces a favorable effect; and  target levels of cholesterol and its fractions are achieved. However, hypolipidemic drugs (HLDs) are prescribed for long-term use, and their prolonged administration may cause various adverse effects. In clinical practice, there are patients with LMD who are resistant to hypolipidemic therapy (HLT), in whom the administration of optimal doses of these drugs does not reduce cholesterol and its fractions to target levels, while increased  preparation dose promotes the development of adverse effects. To optimize the treatment of such patients, we combined laser therapy and therapeutic unloading exercises. 58 patients with CAD and LMD resistant to HLT were examined. At the baseline, depending on the treatment modality,  patients were divided into two comparable groups according to their clinical and functional characteristics and maintenance drug therapy: main group (MG) ( 29 patients) received a combination of laser therapy (intravenous laser blood irradiation, ILBI, and cutaneous exposure to infrared laser radiation) and kinesitherapy in the form of therapeutic unloading exercises (TUE);  control group (CG) – 29 patients continued to receive basic medicamentous therapy. Results of data obtained  indicate a significant hypolipidemic effect after treatment  in the main group (1 and 3 months of follow-up); these patients   received ILBI and external infrared laser therapy sessions  in combination with physical unloading  rehabilitation. One and three- month follow-up in  this group showed a significant reduction of total cholesterol (TC by 27.9% and 33.2%, respectively) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C by 34.0% and 42.6%, respectively) as well as significant increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C by 28.2% and 29.9%, respectively),  significant decrease in the atherogenic index (AI by 51.1% and 57.5%, respectively) and triglyceride levels (TG by 47.1% and 47.7%, respectively). At the same time, no significant changes in the lipid profile dynamics were observed in the control group in 1 and 3 months after the treatment.</jats:p>

title: Resonant Excitation of the Boundary Distortion of a Cold Semi-Infinite Plasma by Electromagnetic Radiation
items.abstract: <jats:p>The effect of external electromagnetic radiation on the curvature of the boundary of a semi-infinite cold plasma, together with the parameters and properties of surface oscillations localized near this boundary, is considered. A new system of two equations has been derived from the known hydrodynamic description of cold electron plasma motion to analyze the nonlinear interaction of a strong electromagnetic field with an electrostatic wave at the plasma surface and with the cavity that appears at the plasma boundary. The self-consistent excitation of electrostatic waves and appearing cavities takes place under certain conditions and may be provided by special choices of initial-boundary magnitudes of perturbation parameters. The corresponding approximate description makes it possible to reveal basic peculiarities of perturbations under consideration and to identify methods of exciting such disturbances of a plasma boundary state. The investigated properties of the surface curvature can be used to obtain current information about the state of the plasma surface and for active influence on it by means, for example, of electromagnetic beams.</jats:p>

title: Long-term outcomes of endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreaticoscopy with contact laser lithotripsy in problematic choledocholithiasis
items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Introduction.</jats:bold>
                    Problematic choledocholithiasis remains one of the most common causes of obstructive jaundice and cholangitis, and the optimal treatment strategy in case of its complex forms is still a matter of debate.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Purpose.</jats:bold>
                    To assess long-term outcomes after endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreaticoscopy (ERCPS) with contact laser lithotripsy in problematic choledocholithiasis and to define its recurrence rate in comparison to traditional surgical options.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Materials and methods.</jats:bold>
                    A multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted in July 2018 - January, 2025. It included 204 patients with problematic choledocholithiasis. Patients were divided into two groups: main group (n = 110) with ERCPS and contact laser lithotripsy, and the control group (n = 94) with choledocholithotomy and Kehr’s T-tube drainage. Surgical access (mini-laparotomy, laparotomy, laparoscopy) was chosen individually according to the clinical situation. The technique efficacy was assessed by the rate of choledocholithiasis recurrence and late complications. Statistical analysis was performed using Mann–Whitney test, χ² test, Kaplan–Meier survival analysis, and non-inferiority analysis.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Results.</jats:bold>
                    Recurrence of choledocholithiasis during three-year follow-up period developed in 11 patients (5.39%): 5.45% in endoscopic group and 5.32% in surgical group (p = 0.789). The recurrence-free three-year period was in 94.6% and 94.7%, respectively (p = 0.977). Late postoperative complications developed in 9.09% of patients after ERCPS and in 12.77% after surgical treatment (p > 0.05). The risk difference for choledocholithiasis recurrence in the long-term postoperative period was -0.001, with an upper 95% confidence interval limit of 5.2% (Δ = 0.10).
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusion.</jats:bold>
                    ERCPS with contact laser lithotripsy is a highly effective and safe method for treating problematic choledocholithiasis which provides low recurrence rate and long-term outcomes comparable to surgical interventions.
                  </jats:p>

title:
Characterisation, simulation and optimisation of a gridless LaB
                    <sub>6</sub>
                    hollow cathode DC plasma source for plasma ion-assisted electron beam deposition of optical coatings
container-title: Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The Plasma Deposition Source (PDS) is a gridless source for plasma ion-assisted deposition (PIAD) of electron beam evaporated optical coatings. PDS geometry, electrical and water-cooling feedthroughs provide a retrofittable configuration to most vacuum deposition chambers. The PDS utilises an inductively heated (100 kHz) LaB
                    <jats:sub>6</jats:sub>
                    hot hollow cathode, providing large-surface-area thermionic emission of a DC glow discharge at low vacuum pressure in the deposition chamber (typically 2 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−4</jats:sup>
                    mbar). The PDS incorporates a pressure differential between axially separated cathode and anode regions, with typical pressures of 2 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    mbar and 2 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−4</jats:sup>
                    mbar, respectively, providing enhanced LaB
                    <jats:sub>6</jats:sub>
                    hollow cathode performance, self-sustaining plasma operation and reduced substrate heat loading and particulate contamination from the cathode. Retarding field energy analyser and Langmuir probe plasma diagnostic measurements and Monte Carlo simulation are described and used to characterise and optimise plasma output and establish fundamental understanding of PDS operation. The PDS provides an optimal ion energy range (5–50 eV) and enhanced ion current density (ICD; ∼0.4 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    at 90 cm distance from the PDS to substrates) suitable for PIAD of densified amorphous optical thin films. Controllable PIAD over an extended deposition area is achieved using a tuneable magnetic field provided by a solenoid formed axially on the exterior of the anode assembly. Automated PDS control is described, providing stable output of plasma ion energy and current density. PIAD of densified single TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and SiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    layers (typical deposition rates of 0.6 and 0.7 nm s
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , respectively) is demonstrated as a function of PDS parameters and plasma ion adatom arrival rate. The influence of the impinging plasma ions is shown to be a thresholding process, where a minimum ICD is required to achieve film densification with a typical ion-to-deposited adatom ratio of ⩾1.2. PIAD of an 11-layer TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    /SiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    multilayer notch filter with no spectral drift over an extended substrate deposition area is also demonstrated.
                  </jats:p>

title: An in situ atmospheric-pressure dielectric barrier discharge setup for time-resolved synchrotron characterisation of cerium metal-organic frameworks
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>In situ</jats:italic>
                    investigation of plasma–material interactions are essential for understanding material stability and transformation mechanisms under non-thermal plasma conditions. Nevertheless, such studies remain challenging due to the limited availability of plasma reactors compatible with synchrotron-based structural and spectroscopic techniques. Here, we present the design, construction, and characterisation of a dedicated
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    atmospheric-pressure dielectric barrier discharge reactor enabling quasi-simultaneous x-ray diffraction (XRD) and x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) during plasma exposure. The compact reactor integrates a quartz discharge tube, an exchangeable powder sample holder, a controlled gas-flow system, and aligned driven and grounded electrodes. The geometry ensures that the reactive gas stream passes directly through the sample while maintaining optical and x-ray access. Stable plasma operation is achieved at 20.8 kHz and peak-to-peak voltages up to 14 kV with various gas mixtures. Electrical diagnostics based on current–voltage measurements and Lissajous analysis quantify discharge power, transferred charge, and effective plasma capacitance, confirming reproducible and tuneable plasma conditions. Optical imaging and thermocouple measurements further validate discharge position in relation to the sample and provide temperature control up to 200 °C. Compatibility with synchrotron radiation investigation is demonstrated at a dedicated beamtime at ESRF (BM23) through time-resolved transmission XAS and XRD measurements. As a proof of concept, cerium-based metal–organic frameworks, Ce-CAU-41 and −44, were investigated, illustrating the capability of the setup to track plasma-induced structural and chemical changes in real time. The developed reactor provides a robust and flexible tool for
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    synchrotron studies of plasma-driven processes and enables mechanistic investigations of material transformations under atmospheric-pressure plasma conditions.
                  </jats:p>

title: Efficient Laser-Diode to Germanate-Tellurite Composite Fiber Excitation via Hyperbolic Microlens on Fiber-Tip
items.abstract: <jats:p>The optimized launch of laser light into an optical fiber is highly important in the field of fiber optics and photonics. In the present work, we investigate the coupling efficiency of a laser diode to the Germanate-Tellurite composite fiber with step and graded refractive index profiles via a hyperbolic microlens formed on the fiber tip. The laser beam propagation is analyzed applying the ABCD matrix formalism; meanwhile, the propagation characteristics of the composite fiber are obtained using the finite difference method. In the current work we numerically compute the fundamental modal field for the estimation of the coupling efficiency, which gives a more accurate calculation of the mode matching. We examine the impact of refractive-index profile, operating wavelengths, core radius, and focal length of the microlens on the coupling performance. The maximum coupling efficiency of about 98–99% is achieved in almost all the core radius values while varying the focal length of the microlens under ideal condition when misalignment is not considered. We also observe that the optimum focal lengths are increasing with the increasing values of core radii in both the step and graded refractive index profiles. We further estimate the coupling efficiency between the laser diode and Germanate-Tellurite composite fiber under both the transverse and angular misalignment conditions and observe that the coupling efficiency is significantly affected by small change in both misalignment values. The proposed approach prescribes the conditions for optimum launch of laser light in Germanate-Tellurite composite fibers and determines the suitability of hyperbolic microlenses for efficient excitation. This model can be readily extended to other soft-glass-based composite fibers which have various applications over the wide wavelength region in linear and nonlinear optics.</jats:p>

title: Phenotypic Age Acceleration and Long‐Term Mortality Across Glycemic States in Peripheral Artery Disease: A Complex Survey Cohort Study
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Peripheral artery disease (PAD) carries high long‐term mortality not fully captured by limb severity or glycemic measures; whether phenotypic age acceleration (PhenoAgeAccel) offers independent prognostic information beyond established risk factors remains unknown. We evaluated PhenoAgeAccel, a routine‐biomarker measure of biological aging, as a marker of cardiometabolic aging in adults with PAD. We analyzed 522 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999–2004 participants with ankle‐brachial index (ABI)‐defined PAD (minimum ABI ≤ 0.90), linked to mortality through 2019 (median follow‐up, 9.9 years). Survey‐weighted Cox models assessed all‐cause and cardiovascular mortality. Glycemic‐status interactions and discrimination were exploratory. During follow‐up, 405 all‐cause and 150 cardiovascular deaths occurred. The highest versus lowest PhenoAgeAccel tertile was associated with all‐cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 3.22; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.37–4.38) and cardiovascular mortality (HR, 3.84; 95% CI, 2.24–6.58). Per standard‐deviation increase, HRs were 1.32 (95% CI, 1.15–1.51) and 1.41 (95% CI, 1.21–1.64), respectively. Adjustment using HbA1c‐informed glycemic status produced similar estimates. Exploratory global interaction
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    values were 0.002 and 0.056, with the largest estimates in the prediabetes‐range group. Adding PhenoAgeAccel increased the apparent Harrell concordance index (C‐index) by 0.021 and 0.016; repeated five‐fold validation yielded mean increments of 0.021 and 0.008. PhenoAgeAccel was associated with long‐term mortality in PAD beyond chronological age and HbA1c‐informed glycemic status. Glycemic‐state heterogeneity was exploratory and requires replication. PhenoAgeAccel remains a candidate prognostic marker rather than a clinically ready tool. Discrimination gains were modest, and cardiovascular prediction showed limited internal stability; external validation and calibration are required before any clinical application.
                  </jats:p>

title: Mezagitamab in immune thrombocytopenia: beyond plasma-cell targeting toward multi-compartment immune modulation
Non-invasive methods of blood glucose control
items.abstract: <jats:p>The authors present the results on reviewing noninvasive glucose monitoring techniques. Special attention was focused on optical ones. More and more efforts of researchers are directed towards the development of noninvasive glucose meter models; however, at the moment there is no any non-invasive medical glucose meter on the market yet. The problem is that developers are trying to achieve the required accuracy of the device. Optical modalities have become the most common ones for noninvasive glucose measurements. Currently, a combination of several methods is more and more popular so as to reduce the error. In the review, the authors describe devices or prototypes of noninvasive glucose meters, principles of their work, areas of analysis and the manufacturing country.</jats:p>

title: Non-Thermal Pretreatments for Hot-Air Drying of Whole Black Chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa): Comparison of Cold Plasma and Indirect Ultrasound
items.abstract: <jats:p>Whole black chokeberries, with their surface wax and firm structure, dry slowly. Atmospheric-pressure cold plasma for 150 or 300 s (CP2.5 and CP5) and indirect ultrasound for 30 min (IUS) were compared before hot-air drying of whole fruit at 50, 60 and 70 °C, with drying duration fixed within each temperature. CP2.5 gave the strongest kinetic response, reducing the time to a moisture ratio of 0.10 (t10) by 19–25%, against 12–17% for CP5 and 11–13% for IUS, and increasing the apparent effective moisture diffusivity by 24–34%. It also gave the lowest mean CIELAB browning index, 64–72% below the control, and the highest mean phenolic, flavonoid and anthocyanin contents among the hot-air-dried groups, with total flavonoid content significantly higher than the control at all temperatures; all remained below the freeze-dried reference. CP5 gave the lowest and IUS the highest shrinkage, and IUS did not differ from the control in composition or antioxidant capacity. Raising the temperature from 50 to 70 °C reduced control t10 by 59%; anthocyanin means were 8–15% lower at 70 °C than at 50 °C. The Arrhenius slopes of the four groups did not differ significantly. Extending plasma exposure reduced the kinetic benefit; the compositional advantage of CP2.5 over CP5 was not statistically demonstrated.</jats:p>

title: Process Optimization for Sustainable Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Stainless Steel
items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) enables the fabrication of complex components through layer-wise manufacturing, offering significant opportunities for improved material utilization and design flexibility. However, identifying sustainable process conditions remains challenging due to the trade-offs between manufacturing performance, environmental impact, economic cost, and social considerations. This study proposes a quantitative Sustainability Index (SI) framework for the integrated assessment and optimization of L-PBF process parameters. The proposed approach combines performance, environmental, and economic indicators into a single optimization objective, enabling sustainability to be directly incorporated into process parameter selection rather than evaluated only as a post-processing criterion. Social considerations are additionally incorporated through a context-dependent assessment to investigate the influence of geographical manufacturing conditions and stakeholder priorities. An experimental dataset comprising 154 L-PBF-manufactured 304L stainless steel specimens produced under different combinations of laser power, scanning speed, and hatch distance was employed to evaluate the proposed framework. Performance was assessed through density and crystallographic isotropy indicators, while environmental and economic aspects were quantified through operational energy consumption and manufacturing-related costs. Multi-Criteria Decision-Making was used to construct the SI, while a regression-tree-based surrogate model and differential evolution optimization algorithm were employed to identify sustainable processing conditions. The results demonstrate that improved sustainability performance is achieved through parameter combinations involving relatively low laser power, high scanning speed, and increased hatch distance, reducing energy consumption and operational costs while maintaining adequate material quality. The optimization procedure consistently identifies improved solutions under different weighting scenarios. Furthermore, the incorporation of country-specific social indicators reveals the influence of regional conditions and sustainability priorities on the final assessment outcomes. The proposed SI provides a quantitative decision-support framework for sustainability-oriented L-PBF optimization and establishes a transferable methodology for future sustainable additive manufacturing applications.</jats:p>

title: SATB1 regulates plasma cell differentiation during T cell-independent immune responses
items.abstract:
<jats:sec>

                    <jats:p>The Special AT-rich binding protein 1 (SATB1) functions as a genome organizer via its ability to modulate 3D-chromatin architecture. SATB1 regulates different programs of gene expression in multiple cell types, including T and B lymphocytes. However, its role in B cell and plasma cell differentiation is still not fully understood.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>
                      Here we investigated the function of SATB1 in plasma cell differentiation by analyzing

                    <jats:p>We found that SATB1-deficiency enhances the differentiation and function of antibody secreting cells during T cell-independent immune responses. title: Erbium-Doped Fiber Laser Q-Switched and Mode-Locked by Red-Fluorescent Carbon-Quantum-Dot-Based Saturable Absorber
items.abstract: <jats:p>A pulsed erbium-doped fiber laser (EDFL) incorporating a saturable absorber (SA) based on red-fluorescent carbon quantum dots (RCQDs) is experimentally demonstrated. First, an RCQD-based, fiber-compatible sandwich-structured SA is fabricated and the nonlinear saturable absorption property (NSAP) is characterized. When the as-prepared RCQDs-SA is integrated into the EDFL with a ring cavity construction, Q-switching and conventional-soliton (CS) mode-locking operations of the laser system are achieved. Stable Q-switching and mode-locking are achieved over pump power ranges of 310–520 mW and 450–590 mW, respectively. In the pump power range of 450–520 mW, the EDFL is robust for switching between Q-switching and mode-locking regimes. The RCQDs-SA exhibits a modulation depth of 11.84% and enables passive Q-switching and passive CS mode-locking when integrated into the EDFL ring cavity. This work, together with our previous ultrafast EDFL mode-locked by green-fluorescent carbon quantum dots (GCQDs) SA, lays a solid foundation for the application and development of carbon quantum dots (CQDs) in the field of ultrafast lasers.</jats:p>

title: Near- and far-field centroid-oscillation diagnostics of straight and curved discharge plasma waveguides
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Discharge capillary plasma waveguides are key components for long-distance laser guiding, multi-GeV laser wakefield acceleration, and staged accelerator coupling. Their optical axis, matched spot size, and effective channel depth directly affect laser guiding quality and beam pointing stability, while in curved waveguides the geometric centerline is not necessarily the optical equilibrium trajectory. Here we extend the established laser centroid-oscillation diagnostic by adding a far-field angular measurement to the conventional near-field exit-position measurement. Combining the two measurements reduces the phase ambiguity of position-only diagnostics and gives a more constrained inversion of the centroid-oscillation phase. In a straight discharge capillary, the two measurements give consistent phases near 154 degrees, corresponding to a matched spot size of about 53.3 μm and an effective channel depth of about 1.25×10
                    <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                    cm
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    under the selected guiding condition. The same diagnostic is applied to a curved capillary with a 1.25 m curvature radius, where the far-field response indicates a preferred nonzero relative injection offset. This combined measurement provides an
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    phase-space diagnostic for straight and curved plasma waveguides.
                  </jats:p>

title: <b>PLATELET-RICH PLASMA (PRP) AS AN ORTHOBIOLOGIC TREATMENT – WHAT DO WE KNOW SO FAR?</b>
items.abstract: <jats:p>In the past decades, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has gained enormous popularity in regenerative medicine, not only as a hair loss and skin-rejuvenation (anti-aging) treatment option but most importantly, as a treatment option for tendon, ligament, muscle and joint injuries, orthopedic post-surgical healing, and osteoarthritis.</jats:p>

title: A tool for comparison of 3D echocardiography generated volume-time-curves
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Volume time curves (VTC) of the left ventricle (LV) generated by three-dimensional echocardiography (3DE) contain information of systolic and diastolic function. We aimed to establish a reference VTC and enable statistical comparison with patient´s VTCs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>VTC of 371 healthy infants, children, and adolescents (age 0–18 years) were used to compute a normalized reference VTC. 43 VTCs of 7 longitudinally studied patients with sick LV in critical aortic stenosis, Shone’s complex, cardiomyopathy in systemic hyperoxalosis, or on a LV assist device were compared to it. Distance metrics defined the degree of deviation from the reference curves in z-scores.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A normalized reference VTC and dV/dt curve was established. Plotting the patient´s VTC against it allowed fast visual perception of differences in the patient´s VTC in concordance with the clinical course. Z-scores showed the degree of deviation for each individual VTC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We generated normalized reference VTC and dV/dt curves for the LV from 3DE-datasets based on a large pediatric cohort. The tool allowed fast visual perception of systolic and diastolic features of patients´ VTC. The degree of shape abnormality of a patient´s VTC was expressed in z-scores. This can serve as a tool for longitudinal follow-up of LV function by acquisition of one 3DE dataset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Impact</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:list list-type="bullet">
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>A normalized left ventricular volume-time curve generated by 3D echocardiography of healthy subjects, in this case children, can be established.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Normalization and establishing a reference curve have not been successful or described so far.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>We provide the code and a graphical user interface tool to perform the normalization of the volume-time curves.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>Patients´ volume-time curves can rapidly be visually and statistically compared to this normalized curve.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                        <jats:list-item>
                          <jats:p>This tool can serve for longitudinal follow-up of left ventricular function, including systolic and diastolic aspects.</jats:p>
                        </jats:list-item>
                      </jats:list>
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Molecular Dipole Engineering Controlling Interlayer Coupling and Centimeter‐Sized Crystal Growth in Polar Perovskites for Broadband Polarization Detection
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Polarization‐sensitive optoelectronic functional crystals have garnered considerable attention owing to their promising applications in optical communication, remote sensing, and military surveillance. In this work, a molecular dipole engineering strategy was employed to grow a centimeter‐sized 2D polar perovskite single crystal (IEA)
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    (MA)Pb
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    I
                    <jats:sub>7</jats:sub>
                    (IEA = iodoethylamine, MA = methylamine). By inducing a prominent molecular dipole on the organic interlayer cations, strong I···I halogen‐halogen interactions are established between the organic cations and the inorganic lead‐halide framework, which drive oriented crystal growth along specific crystallographic directions. Notably, the molecular dipole engineering imparts pronounced polar character and structural anisotropy to the crystals, thereby enabling self‐powered polarization‐sensitive photoresponse even at zero bias. The photodetector fabricated from these single crystals exhibits self‐powered polarization detection capability across the visible to near‐infrared broad spectral range, with an excellent polarization ratio and fast response speed. This work provides a facile and efficient molecular design strategy for preparing large‐sized anisotropic perovskite single crystals, which is conducive to advancing the development of self‐powered broadband polarization‐sensitive optoelectronic devices.

Experimental investigation of laser engraving parameters for QR code marking on AISI 304 stainless steel sheet
items.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Context—The increasing diversity and production volume of industrial products have heightened the need for reliable, low-cost traceability methods throughout the product life cycle. QR codes offer an important alternative for product identification and traceability due to their high data capacity and low implementation cost. Although direct QR code marking provides permanent identification on metallic surfaces, metal reflectivity and laser-induced surface characteristics can affect readability. Therefore, determining suitable laser parameters for rapid and reliable QR code generation on metal surfaces is an important research topic.Objective—The objective of this study is to investigate the readability of QR codes produced by laser engraving on AISI 304 stainless steel sheet using a smartphone camera and to determine suitable process conditions in terms of laser power, laser speed, and scan offset parameters.Method—Experimental studies were conducted using a Snapmaker Artisan 3-in-1 device equipped with a 40 W blue diode laser operating at an approximate wavelength of 450 nm. AISI 304 stainless steel sheet with a thickness of 0.5 mm was used as the material. Preliminary studies determined that the smallest QR code size readable using a commonly available smartphone camera with a resolution of 12 MP was 20 × 20 mm. In the experimental design, laser power levels of 30%, 50%, 80%, and 100%; laser speeds of 2500, 5000, 7500, and 10000 mm/min; and scan offset values of 0 and 0.2 were selected. The readability of QR codes produced using different parameter combinations was evaluated using a smartphone camera.Results—At a scan offset of 0, none of the QR codes produced at 30% laser power were readable, while readability generally improved with increasing laser power and decreasing laser speed. At the highest speed (10000 mm/min), no QR codes were readable. Increasing the scan offset to 0.2 significantly improved camera-based readability despite only a slight visual improvement in sharpness. Four previously unreadable parameter combinations became readable, demonstrating that even a small change in scan offset can substantially influence QR code readability depending on laser power and speed.Conclusion—The results demonstrate that laser power, laser speed, and scan offset should be considered together when producing QR codes on AISI 304 stainless steel using laser engraving. A scan offset of 0.2 improved QR code readability with a smartphone camera and enabled successful marking across a wider process-parameter range. These findings support the use of low-cost diode laser systems for industrial product traceability and direct part marking. Future studies may examine different materials, larger QR data sets, and image-processing systems simulating moving production lines.</jats:p>

title: Photodynamic therapy for skin cancer in the auricles
items.abstract: <jats:p>Skin cancer of the auricle is the 5th most common malignant tumor of the skin of the head and neck. Treatment of malignant skin tumors in this location is a difficult task due to the complex anatomy of this organ, the difficulty of obtaining a satisfactory cosmetic result, and the high risk of relapse. Therefore, when choosing the optimal method for treating ear skin cancer, taking into account the functional and cosmetic significance of this area, preference should be given to low-trauma and organ-preserving options, which include the photodynamic therapy (PDT) method. This paper presents the results of a retrospective analysis of 38 patients with basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin of the auricle who underwent photodynamic therapy. Complete regression of tumor foci after one course of PDT was recorded in 32 patients (84.2%), partial regression — in 6 patients (15.8%) who underwent the 2nd course, achieving a complete response. During the observed period, relapse of the disease was diagnosed in 3 patients with T2-3 prevalence. This technique is an effective method of local control with good and acceptable cosmetic results and can be an alternative to surgical intervention in cases where surgery is impossible or undesirable.</jats:p>

title: Theoretical and Experimental Demonstration of Trace Enantiomer Sensing via Chiral Flux in Aperture Tetramers Metasurfaces
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chiral sensing is of great significance in biology, medicine, and chemistry, with metasurfaces being an ideal platform for enhancing molecular chiral responses. However, the improvement of trace detection performance urgently demands exploration of novel metasurface‐based sensing mechanisms. Most existing strategies rely on circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy, while monitoring near‐field superchiral fields, which directly interact with analytes and encode richer chiral information, has great potential for higher detection efficiency. Nevertheless, this strategy is limited by near‐field detection difficulties and strict metasurface design criteria. Here, a novel chiral‐flux‐based strategy is proposed to discriminate trace chiral enantiomers and is comprehensively verified via theoretical analysis, numerical simulation and experiment. A uniquely designed aperture tetramer metasurface generates a single‐sign superchiral field that directly interacts with analytes and yields over 40‐fold enhancement. Chiral analytes will induce an asymmetric field perturbation under circularly polarized light, which can be quantified by far‐field chiral flux following optical chirality conservation. Consistent with numerical simulations and coupled dipole model analysis, experiments on penicillamine enantiomers validate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. A minimum distinguishable concentration of 0.1 µg/µL is experimentally observed. Distinct from traditional CD spectroscopy, this method paves a new pathway for high‐sensitivity trace chiral detection.</jats:p>

title: Fiber‐Delivered Photothermal Self‐Oscillation Sustained by Thermal‐Memory Feedback at Confined Air–Water Interfaces
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Light‐driven self‐oscillators convert steady optical energy into autonomous periodic motion, but most existing systems rely on free‐space illumination and open environments, restricting their operation in confined or optically shielded spaces. Here, we demonstrate fiber‐delivered photothermal self‐oscillation at confined air–water interfaces using a dual‐zone thin‐film actuator. Near‐infrared light guided through a flexible multimode optical fiber is redistributed by a ZnO/PDMS scattering zone and converted into heat in an adjacent C/PDMS photothermal zone, thereby generating Marangoni propulsion without direct line‐of‐sight illumination. Co‐moving infrared thermography shows that the temperature difference between water‐surface ROIs on opposite sides of the film is larger during the forward stroke than during the return stroke, indicating that the local thermal state under constant optical input depends on the direction of motion. Together with the experimentally measured finite thermal‐relaxation time, transient thermo‐fluid‐Marangoni simulations reveal distinct forward and return branches of the driving force at the same actuator position. These results support a feedback mechanism in which thermal‐memory‐dependent driving and elastic recovery of the optical fiber jointly sustain the oscillation. A semi‐empirical trend model calibrated using power‐dependent experiments further captures the primary effects of optical power, film dimensions, and free fiber length on the steady‐state peak‐to‐peak displacement. As a proof of concept, an integrated micropillar array enables the oscillator to capture floating objects inside a dark pipeline‐like environment. This fiber‐enabled optothermofluidic strategy extends light‐driven self‐oscillation beyond free‐space optical access and provides a route toward autonomous soft machines operating in confined liquid environments.</jats:p>

title: Engineering the decoherence-free interaction for giant atoms with multiple coupling points in semi-infinite waveguide-QED systems
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Giant atoms, a new paradigm beyond local coupling in quantum optics, have been shown to interact without decohering via different types of waveguides. Notably, when coupled to a one-dimensional (1D) semi-infinite waveguide, giant atoms in braided and nested configurations-characterized by their coupling points that are spatially braided or nested-can both exhibit the decoherence-free interaction (DFI). However, previous work involving 1D semi-infinite waveguides and giant atoms has only considered the case of giant atoms with two coupling points each. In this work, we analyze the behavior of two giant atoms coupled to a 1D semi-infinite waveguide via multiple coupling points each. We demonstrate that the DFI between two giant atoms in braided and nested configurations remains feasible in the case where each atom has multiple coupling points. In particular, we have derived the quantitative relation between the number of coupling points and the phase shift values for which DFI can be achieved. Furthermore, we find that the DFI strength also varies with the number of coupling points, and its maximally achievable value increases as the number of coupling points increases. Finally, we demonstrate that the DFI can also be realized in systems consisting of multiple giant atoms with multiple coupling points each. These results may have potential applications in quantum simulation and quantum information processing.</jats:p>

title: Radiation monitoring in the scattered field of a clinical electron FLASH beam with Timepix4
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>FLASH radiotherapy is an emerging technique, delivered at
  ultra-high dose rates, that holds promise for improving the
  treatment of certain cancers. Resolving the pulse structure of the
  beam is a major challenge in the primary field, where the extreme
  particle flux prevents accurate pulse-resolved measurements. Even in
  the scattered field, few instruments provide the precision required
  for radiation protection and beam monitoring. Single-particle
  counting detectors offer a way forward: the Timepix family of hybrid
  pixel detectors records each particle interaction individually, with
  its time of arrival and time over threshold. This work reports a
  first evaluation of a Timepix4 assembly bonded to a 300 μm
  p-on-n sensor in the scattered field of a clinical electron beam,
  inside and outside of the treatment room, at the Mobetron facility
  (CHUV, Lausanne), using a 9 MeV beam delivered at conventional
  (∼ 0.5 Gy/s) and high (30–230 Gy/s) dose rates. Individual
  beam pulses were resolved and counted in both modes, with repetition
  frequencies consistent with the machine settings. Within high dose
  rate pulses, progressive data loss from readout saturation distorts
  the recorded pulse shape, so the intra-pulse profile is not
  reliable, while pulse counting and timing are unaffected. Outside
  the treatment room, where passive dosimeters record only background,
  individual pulses were still resolved in high-dose-rate mode. These
  results establish Timepix4 as a viable pulse-resolved detector for
  radiation protection and out-of-field monitoring in FLASH RT,
  reliably resolving pulse timing and counts even at dose levels below
  what passive dosimeters can register.</jats:p>

title: Analysis of modulation transfer function in large-field-of-view pulsed radiation imaging systems: component contributions and magnification effects
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pulsed radiation imaging systems are essential diagnostics
  in high-energy-density physics, inertial confinement fusion, Z-pinch
  experiments, and flash X-ray radiography. These systems typically
  consist of a cascaded chain: a thick pinhole, scintillator, optical
  lens, gated image intensifier, fiber optic taper, and camera. The
  overall spatial resolution is jointly determined by the modulation
  transfer functions (MTFs) of individual components and their
  coupling under various magnifications. However, most existing
  studies focus on single components, and a system-level theoretical
  framework that integrates the component-level MTFs for such pulsed
  radiation imaging chains remains lacking. In this work, we propose a
  system-level analysis framework based on component-level MTF
  modeling. We integrate MTF models of the thick pinhole (ray
  tracing), scintillator (Geant4 simulation), optical lens, gated
  image intensifier, fiber optic taper, and camera, and construct a
  comprehensive system MTF expression. The effects of key parameters
  — pinhole magnification, image intensifier size, and the number of
  camera pixels — on the limiting object-plane resolution are
  systematically analyzed. Results show that pinhole magnification is
  the dominant factor: when magnification increases from 0.5×
  to 2.0×, the limiting object-plane resolution (at 5%
  contrast) improves from 1.2 lp/mm to 2.63 lp/mm. In contrast, for
  the configurations studied, increasing the image intensifier
  diameter from 18 mm to 40 mm yields less than 3% improvement, and
  increasing the number of camera pixels beyond
  2K× 2K gives negligible benefit for the
  baseline configuration. This work identifies resolution bottlenecks
  under different configurations and provides a practical theoretical
  tool for system parameter optimization in pulsed radiation imaging
  diagnostics.</jats:p>

title: Strong enough to go home
Nonlinear reaction–convection–diffusion in porous catalyst pellets: dead-core formation, effectiveness and transport regimes
Research and Application of Nitrogen Foam Huff-N-Puff Technology in Strong Bottom-Water Reservoirs
items.abstract: <jats:p>Fault-block sandstone reservoirs with strong bottom water commonly experience rapid bottom-water coning, incomplete well patterns, and inefficient mobilization of attic oil. This study investigated the oil-displacement and water-control mechanisms of nitrogen foam huff-n-puff and optimized its injection–production parameters using single-well physical-model experiments, refined three-dimensional numerical simulation, and a field pilot test. Nitrogen migrated toward structural highs through gravity segregation and pressure diffusion, providing pressure support and mobilizing attic oil through gas expansion. Foam was preferentially retained in high-permeability bottom-water channels, where the Jamin effect increased water-flow resistance. Laboratory experiments identified simultaneous gas–liquid injection, a gas–liquid ratio of 2:1, injection at the top of the oil zone, and controlled low-rate production after reopening as favorable conditions, with total recovery factors of 43.18%, 42.08%, and 49.81% in the preferred injection-timing, gas–liquid-ratio, and post-soak production-strategy cases, respectively. Thirty-two numerical cases with three factors at four levels gave an economically favorable gas injection rate of 5 × 104 m3·d−1, cumulative nitrogen injection of 1.0 × 106 m3 per cycle, and a soak time of 20 d. Two field cycles in a single horizontal well (Well A1) injected 1.0 × 106 m3 of nitrogen and produced 1100 t of treatment-associated incremental oil (sensitivity range 865–1100 t depending on the counterfactual production baseline), with a weighted treatment cost of CNY 727/t, 20.0% lower than the numerical estimate. These findings support the potential for coordinated upper-zone oil displacement and lower-zone water control at the pilot scale. In the field case, the well was shut in for approximately 65 months prior to the first huff-and-puff cycle. Production continued before the second cycle, albeit at a low rate of 1.9 tons per day. Following the second huff-and-puff cycle, production declined further to 0.6 tons per day at the end of the cycle, prompting the initiation of a third cycle. Hence, the laboratory experiments, numerical optimization, and field pilot test proceeded as mutually informed components of an integrated study rather than as a strictly sequential design–validation chain.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence, Motivation, and Burnout Among Radiologists and Radiation Oncologists
container-title: Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Burnout is a major concern across medical professions, with radiologists and radiation oncologists among the most affected. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to reduce burnout by decreasing workload; however, previous research has shown inconsistent associations between AI use and burnout. These relationships may depend on clinicians' motivation for using AI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 6.5 min anonymous online survey was distributed to members of the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists (RANZCR) over a 2 month period (May–July 2025). Measures included demographics and work‐related variables (hours, level of training), burnout, AI use (frequency and task type), and motivation to use AI (based on Self‐Determination Theory). Motivation was examined as a moderator of the relationship between AI use and burnout.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Responses were received from 121 clinicians (90 radiologists, 31 radiation oncologists), including 21 trainees. Clinically significant burnout was reported by 42.1% (51/121) of respondents. Ninety‐one (75.2%) respondents reported using AI, primarily for image analysis and interpretation (radiologists) and treatment planning (radiation oncologists). There was no overall significant relationship between AI use and burnout. However, AI use was positively associated with burnout among those reporting lower autonomy in AI use. This relationship was not mediated by need satisfaction or frustration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI use is common among RANZCR members, and the burnout rate is prevalent. These preliminary findings highlight the potential importance of supporting autonomous motivation when implementing AI, while recognising that larger and more context‐specific studies are required to confirm this relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A bionic strong and tough amphibious adhesive inspired by barnacles and articular cartilage
items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Developing strong and tough amphibious adhesives that can achieve high adhesion strength in both dry and wet environments remains a major challenge. Herein, inspired by the hydrophobic–hydrophilic adhesion strategy of barnacle cement proteins and the fibre-reinforced load-bearing structure of articular cartilage, a bioinspired polyurethane adhesive (TA@WS2/PU) with strong, tough, and durable underwater adhesion was developed. In this system, catechol-containing chain extenders were introduced to provide robust substrate anchoring, while fluorinated polyimide segments induced pronounced microphase separation and generated low-surface-energy hydrophobic nanodomains for interfacial dewetting. Furthermore, tannic-acid-modified tungsten disulfide nanosheets (TA@WS2) were incorporated into the optimized polyurethane matrix to construct a cartilage-mimetic reinforcing network, in which high-aspect-ratio nanosheets acted as load-bearing skeletons and tannic-acid-rich surfaces formed dense hydrogen-bonding interactions with polyurethane chains. The resulting 10%-TA@WS2/PU adhesive (the addition of TA@WS2 is 10 wt.%) exhibited a tensile strength of 108 MPa, elongation at break of 1150%, and toughness of 371 MJ·m−3, together with a dry lap-shear strength of 9.6 MPa on Fe substrates. More importantly, it achieved an underwater lap-shear strength of 4.2 MPa and maintained excellent interfacial stability during prolonged aqueous exposure. Multiscale analyses across molecular, microscopic, and macroscopic scales revealed that the superior underwater adhesion originated from the cooperative effects of hydration-layer disruption, exposed adhesive groups, compact microphase-separated packing, and nanosheet-induced diffusion barriers. This dual-bioinspired strategy provides a promising route for developing strong, tough, durable, and recyclable amphibious adhesives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

The Weakening of Strong Verbs in Norwegian, Swedish, and Icelandic: A Comparative Study
items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    This article combines a diachronic and a comparative approach to examine the development of strong verbs in the North Germanic languages Norwegian, Swedish, and Icelandic, complementing prior research on weakening in West Germanic languages. Using quantitative methods, we assess the impact of token frequency, class, and ablaut pattern on weakening. The results reveal that Norwegian and Swedish exhibit substantially more weakening than Icelandic, especially in their participles. This sets them apart from West Germanic languages, which show more weakening in the preterite. This discrepancy between North and West Germanic languages can likely be attributed to North Germanic languages being comparatively less exposed to
                    <jats:italic>Präteritumschwund</jats:italic>
