items.abstract: <jats:p>We introduce a group-action-based mechanism that converts a crisp subset [Formula: see text] into an induced fuzzy set by measuring, for each [Formula: see text], the proportion of the orbit of [Formula: see text] that intersects [Formula: see text]. This orbit-density membership is constant on orbits, admits sharp min–max bounds under subgroup refinement, provides a symmetry-induced alternative to classical rough membership, and is compatible with equivariant maps under mild bijectivity/measure-compatibility assumptions. To remove finiteness restrictions, we extend the construction to measurable [Formula: see text]-spaces by replacing orbit cardinalities with an orbit probability system [Formula: see text], yielding a measure-based membership [Formula: see text] that preserves the structural invariance principles of the finite setting. We further propose a simple sanity-check and observability protocol: if the chosen observable is already [Formula: see text]-invariant, the induced membership collapses to a crisp decision, whereas non-invariant observables generically produce nontrivial boundary regions. A numerical illustration on a permutation-symmetry model is included to demonstrate how the framework distinguishes invariant versus observable features in an orbit-structured uncertainty model.</jats:p>

title: Balancing the Energy Trilemma in Decentralised Energy Systems: A Systematic Literature Review of CER Ecosystems
items.abstract: <jats:p>Consumer Energy Resources (CER) are fundamentally transforming energy systems, shifting energy generation from a cohort of centralised power plants towards a prosumer-centric, decentralised and democratised energy network. Once limited to passive rooftop solar photovoltaic systems, advancements in CER now enable households to actively consume, produce and export electricity. While the proliferation of CER supports global decarbonisation objectives, it simultaneously adds pressure to energy equity and energy security objectives. The stochastic nature of CER, shaped by consumer behaviour and diurnal variations, increases variability in electricity generation and demand, undermining the predictability traditionally required for a reliable and resilient energy system. The uneven deployment of CER technologies may also exacerbate energy inequities, while increased digitalisation introduces new vulnerabilities, including cyberattacks, coordination failures and reduced system observability. Existing institutional and regulatory frameworks remain largely oriented towards centralised power plants and are insufficiently equipped to coordinate the complexities of a decentralised energy system. Without effective coordination, increasing CER penetration risks destabilising energy systems at scale, threatening energy reliability and the delivery of electricity as an essential service. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review and thematic analysis of the interactions between prosumers, CER technologies and the ecosystem in which they operate. The review develops a consumer-centred CER ecosystem framework comprising three interconnected dimensions: contextual influences, CER technologies and operational arrangements, and governance and institutional mechanisms. The synthesis identifies how interactions between these dimensions influence access and participation, operational coordination, and the distribution of benefits and risks. The findings demonstrate that the contribution of CER to the energy trilemma is dependent not only on technological capabilities, but also on consumer characteristics, governance structures and institutional arrangements. The proposed framework provides a conceptual foundation for examining potential synergies and trade-offs between energy trilemma objectives and identifies opportunities for further empirical investigation into the governance arrangements that support equitable, secure and environmentally sustainable CER integration.</jats:p>

title: Intergranular and microstructural evolution regulates mechanical and ion-transport properties of NaSICON-type solid electrolytes
items.abstract: <jats:p>Ionic transport and mechanical integrity are critical to the performance of ceramic solid electrolytes in solid-state batteries. Although grain-boundary engineering improves ionic transport, its effects on mechanical properties remain unclear. Here, the impact of nominal LaNbO<sub>4</sub> (LN) additions on the mechanical properties and ionic transport behavior of the solid electrolyte Na<sub>3.4</sub>Zr<sub>2</sub>Si<sub>2.4</sub>P<sub>0.6</sub>O<sub>12</sub> (NZSP) is investigated. The results show that LN reacts with NZSP during processing, forming Na<sub>3</sub>LaP<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8 </sub>and Nb-rich intergranular regions. The Na<sub>3</sub>LaP<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8 </sub>phase affects the microstructure by reducing grain-size heterogeneity and limiting microcrack formation, while the Nb-rich intergranular regions, distributed along grain boundaries and residual pores, may contribute to improved densification. Among the samples examined, the NZSP sample with 2 mol% LN exhibits enhanced mechanical properties together with a 79% increase in ionic conductivity; compared with the unmodified sample, the elastic modulus, hardness, and fracture toughness increase by approximately 14%, 40%, and 82%, respectively, while the mean fracture strength is approximately 11% higher. With further increases in LN content, the ionic conductivity decreases, while the fracture toughness of 10LN falls below that of 2LN and 5LN but remains higher than that of pristine NZSP. These findings highlight the influence of LN-induced microstructural evolution on mechanical properties and ionic transport in the investigated NZSP samples, providing insights into the development of NaSICON-type solid electrolytes for solid-state sodium batteries.</jats:p>

title: Lightweight UAV Fruit Detection for Clustered and Occluded Objects: Density-Aware Reasoning from Geometry-Consistent Representations
container-title: Journal of Progress in Engineering and Physical Science
items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate fruit detection from UAV imagery is importance for yield estimation. However, this task remains challenging in real-world applications, as fruits are typically small in size, densely clustered, and frequently occluded by tree canopies. Under such complex conditions, the overlap suppression mechanisms adopted in existing detection methods often lack explicit modeling of density context, resulting in limited adaptability to densely small-object scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight UAV-based fruit detection framework that introduces density-aware overlap reasoning, supported by geometry-consistent representations to enhance detection reliability. Specifically, a space-to-depth convolution (SPD-Conv) is incorporated at the early downsampling stages of the backbone to preserve fine-grained structural details of small objects. Meanwhile, a self-supervised equivariant attention mechanism (SEAM) is introduced as a regularization constraint, enabling the model to stably focus on instance-level structures under viewpoint variations and partial occlusions, thereby providing reliable geometric cues for subsequent decision making. At the inference stage, we introduce a density-aware overlap reasoning strategy that continuously models local instance density via soft-count IoU aggregation and integrates bounded-influence suppression to limit excessive penalties from extreme overlaps, alleviating systematic over-suppression while preserving true neighboring detections in densely clustered scenes. We conduct representative case studies on a self-built UAV orchard dataset and public fruit detection benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing lightweight detectors.</jats:p>

title: A modular simulation framework for multidirectional interaction modeling in cell transmission models
items.abstract: <jats:p>Modeling multidirectional pedestrian flows within a cell transmission model requires a representation that distinguishes the different movements simultaneously occupying a shared cell. Existing cell transmission model extensions can represent commodities, routes, turning movements, or movement directions, but the locally relevant interaction structure within a cell is not always made explicit. This paper introduces a graph-based movement-state representation in which each pedestrian movement is characterized by its predecessor cell, current cell, and successor cell. This representation explicitly identifies potentially interacting movements and provides a common basis for specifying and calibrating movement-specific sending functions without prescribing a particular interaction model. Using controlled pedestrian flow scenarios generated with PTV Vissim, we calibrate and compare a parametric interaction model and a machine learning-based model across different demand combinations. Both interaction-aware models reproduce the microsimulation-generated outflows more accurately than a no-interaction baseline, with the machine learning model achieving the highest predictive accuracy when sufficiently broad calibration data are available, albeit at increased computational cost compared with the analytical formulation. Additional multi-cell experiments show that, under unconstrained downstream conditions, locally calibrated sending functions can be embedded in a cell transmission model network containing a single calibrated interaction cell while retaining the standard cell transmission model formulation in adjacent cells. The proposed framework therefore provides a transparent and modular basis for representing, calibrating, and embedding localized multidirectional interactions in cell transmission model-based pedestrian simulations.</jats:p>

title: Plasma Cell Leukemia: Aggressive Disease Hidden in Plasma Cell Biology
items.abstract: <jats:p>Plasma cell leukemia (PCL) represents the most aggressive manifestation of plasma cell neoplasia. Despite sharing a common cellular origin and numerous molecular features with multiple myeloma (MM), PCL exhibits a strikingly different biological behavior that is characterized by the ability of malignant plasma cells to escape the bone-marrow niche, survive in circulation, and disseminate to extramedullary sites. Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying this transition may provide important insights into the aggressive nature of the disease. This review focuses on alterations occurring within malignant plasma cells and examines how they distinguish leukemic plasma cells from their counterparts in conventional multiple myeloma. Particular attention is given to their changes in cellular adhesion and homing, interactions with the bone-marrow microenvironment, proliferative activity, apoptotic regulation, and cellular adaptation to survival outside the protective marrow niche. By integrating genomic, transcriptomic, immunophenotypic, and microenvironmental findings, we explore the biological similarities and differences between PCL and conventional MM. Furthermore, we discuss how advances in molecular characterization have influenced prognostic risk stratification and the development of biologically directed therapeutic strategies, including targeted agents and T-cell-redirecting immunotherapies. Connecting these biological insights with emerging clinical evidence may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of PCL and support the development of more effective, disease-specific therapeutic approaches.</jats:p>

The PDS provides an optimal ion energy range (5–50 eV) and enhanced ion current density (ICD; ∼0.4 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    at 90 cm distance from the PDS to substrates) suitable for PIAD of densified amorphous optical thin films. Controllable PIAD over an extended deposition area is achieved using a tuneable magnetic field provided by a solenoid formed axially on the exterior of the anode assembly. Automated PDS control is described, providing stable output of plasma ion energy and current density. PIAD of densified single TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and SiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    layers (typical deposition rates of 0.6 and 0.7 nm s
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , respectively) is demonstrated as a function of PDS parameters and plasma ion adatom arrival rate. The influence of the impinging plasma ions is shown to be a thresholding process, where a minimum ICD is required to achieve film densification with a typical ion-to-deposited adatom ratio of ⩾1.2. PIAD of an 11-layer TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    /SiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    multilayer notch filter with no spectral drift over an extended substrate deposition area is also demonstrated.
                  </jats:p>

title: Packing geometry, not signal strength, limits the targeting precision of a migrating cell population: A minimal self-propelled particle model
container-title: International Journal of Modern Physics C
items.abstract:
<jats:p>Collective cell migration is a fundamental process in embryonic development, wound healing, and cancer invasion. Most theoretical work has asked whether a migrating cell population moves at all; comparatively little attention has gone to how precisely it can converge on a small, localized target once directed motion is already established. To address this question, we build a deliberately minimal particle-based model in which each cell is a self-propelled agent whose polarity vector (taken, as a simplifying assumption, to directly set its migration direction) is reoriented by a chemoattractant gradient subject to signal shielding among crowded neighbors, by short-range excluded-volume repulsion with its neighbors, and by stochastic fluctuations. Cells are not coupled through polarity alignment, co-attraction, or adhesion: the population is better described as a set of independently chemotactic agents coupled only through mechanical exclusion and mutual signal occlusion.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Using this model, we find that adding short-range steric repulsion between cells, even at strengths thousands of times weaker than our reference value (down to the smallest value tested, [Formula: see text]), converts a population that would otherwise converge essentially perfectly onto a chemoattractant source into one whose cells remain, on average, at a substantial, finite distance from it. The population’s centre of mass nevertheless reaches the target, and the population settles into a stationary configuration in which individual cells keep moving and rearranging: the finite mean distance reflects the spatial extent of a packed cluster rather than a failure of the population to arrive. The onset is largely abrupt (most of the effect is already present at the smallest repulsion strength tested) and grows only gradually with further increases in repulsion strength; over the ranges of noise amplitude, chemotactic strength, and gradient length scale that we tested, the mean distance is not appreciably shifted. Instead, it scales with the square root of population size (up to [Formula: see text]), with a prefactor within about 5% of an independent, elementary two-dimensional close-packing estimate. We interpret this as a packing-limited phenomenon: a direct geometric consequence of combining mutual exclusion with convergent guidance, which we do not characterize further with structural or dynamical jamming diagnostics (such as the pair correlation function, mean-squared displacement, or contact number) and therefore do not claim as evidence of a genuine jamming transition in the statistical-physics sense. We further show that an additional, explicitly imposed restoring force toward the group’s center of mass—intended to caricature tissue-scale mechanical cohesion, which is not otherwise present in the model—is either redundant with the population’s natural packing-limited footprint (when its characteristic radius exceeds that footprint) or catastrophic (when tighter, effectively freezing the population near its starting position by competing with and overriding the chemotactic cue).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Together, these results indicate that steric exclusion and population size, rather than being secondary modulators of collective migration efficiency, can dominate how precisely a cell population lands on a localized target, over a parameter range in which neither chemotactic strength nor noise amplitude does. We discuss the relevance of this packing-limited stalling for biological scenarios that require precise collective homing, such as stem-cell niche occupancy or immune-cell recruitment to a localized site, and outline the model’s limitations, including the polarity-velocity identification, the absence of independent jamming diagnostics, and the restricted sense in which this model is “collective.”</jats:p>

SARS-CoV-2 exposure induces plasma cell expansion but T cell depletion associated with PANoptosis-related molecular signatures in human lymphoid tissues
items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SARS-CoV-2 infection induces immune dysfunction in secondary lymphoid organs; however, whether SARS-CoV-2 directly causes intrinsic immune injury within these lymphoid compartments remains elusive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Spatial transcriptomic sequencing (ST-seq) was performed on hilar lymph node specimens from fatal COVID-19 patients. Human tonsil immune organoids (TOs) were constructed and exposed ex vivo to the original strain of SARS-CoV-2 (OVS) and the Omicron XBB.1.5 variant. Integrated analyses combining single-nucleus random sequencing (snRandom-seq) and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) were used to characterize cellular subsets and cytokine production.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ST-seq revealed robust plasma cell accumulation accompanied by severe T cell depletion in COVID-19 lymph nodes. In TOs, SARS-CoV-2 exposure was associated with the differentiation of germinal center (GC) B cells into antibody-secreting plasma cells. Viral exposure markedly enhanced the secretion of proinflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IFN-γ, and IL-2) in both CD4
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      and CD8
                      <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                      T cells, even though SARS-CoV-2 viral mRNA was undetectable in TOs. Persistent inflammatory cascades were accompanied by upregulation of PANoptosis-associated molecular signatures, including NLRP3, Caspase-8, and MLKL. Notably, none of these phenotypic alterations were observed in influenza virus-infected TOs.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SARS-CoV-2 exposure is associated with aberrant plasma cell differentiation and upregulation of PANoptosis-associated molecular signatures via inflammatory overactivation, potentially contributing to T cell depletion and systemic immune dysfunction during COVID-19 pathogenesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Advanced Surface Coatings for Biosensors: A Review of Atmospheric Plasma Innovations
items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Biosensing relies on the precise engineering of the bio‐interface to achieve good performance (e.g., sensitivity, working range, stability) in complex samples. Despite their favorable properties, metals, polymers, carbon nanotubes, and paper remain challenging biosensing substrates due to surface inertness, biofouling, and poor biomolecule adhesion. Wet‐chemical modification can address these limitations but is frequently hindered by multi‐step protocols, chemical waste, and substrate‐specific constraints. This review demonstrates plasma as a versatile, more sustainable, and dry‐state alternative for the advanced (bio)functionalization of biosensor surfaces. Atmospheric plasma is discussed as a universal toolkit for creating high‐performance interfaces, including bioreceptor immobilization, engineered roughness, anti‐biofouling layers, and stabilization for shelf‐life by depositing tailored ultra‐thin films to enhance biosensor performance, essential for the next generation of biosensors.</jats:p>

title: Ubiquitous Simulation Objects in Parallel Discrete Event Simulation on NUMA Platforms
container-title: ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation
items.abstract: <jats:p>One of the characteristics of modern multiprocessor machines is Non-Uniform-Memory-Access (NUMA). It has been integrated in the chipset in order to enable scalability of memory accesses by different CPUs to different RAM zones, in particular the NUMA-local ones. At the same time, NUMA-remote zones of memory are accessed with higher latency and imposing higher traffic on the interconnection network across memory components. We face this problem in the context of Parallel Discrete Event Simulation (PDES) by proposing a ubiquity-based solution where the state of any simulation object is present at any time instant in all (or multiple) NUMA-nodes. It can therefore be accessed by the CPU running a worker thread of the PDES engine exploiting NUMA locality. Our solution provides the support for managing the object-state replicas transparently via instrumentation and operating system services. Also, it allows the exploitation of the natural read-intensiveness of real-world workloads for making the cost to update the state replicas negligible. Our solution addresses the core problem related to the impossibility of optimizing (either statically or dynamically) the placement of simulation objects (their states) on the different NUMA-nodes. This is typical in scenarios of non-isotropic variable workloads along the simulation time axis. We integrated our NUMA-ubiquity proposal in the open source PARSIR (PARallel SImulation Runner) platform, which has been recently developed for effectively running PDES on top of shared-memory multiprocessor machines and Posix/Linux operating systems.</jats:p>

Outcomes of an Interprofessional Intensive Care In Situ Simulation Program Over a Five-year Period
container-title: Simulation in Healthcare: The Journal of the Society for Simulation in Healthcare
items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Translational and in situ simulation activities improve clinical performance, identify latent patient safety threats, and test systems and processes. However, there are few examples of established, sustained translational simulation programs, particularly in intensive care unit (ICU) settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We collected data on an interprofessional in situ simulation program in a tertiary ICU between February 2021 and December 2025. Educational, quality assurance, feasibility, and sustainability outcomes were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 790 clinicians provided feedback over the 5-year study period. A total of 203 in situ simulation sessions were scheduled, with 168 (82.8%) of these sessions run. The proportion of cancelled sessions decreased steadily from 33.3% in 2021 to 9.1% in 2025 (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.016). Over 99% of respondents felt that in situ simulation training was “very helpful” (86.8%) or “helpful” (13.0%) for their clinical practice. There was no statistically significant difference in participant perceptions between the 7 different scenarios (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.98). There were no reported incidences of participants feeling psychologically unsafe and no episodes of participant refusal. Three new ICU protocols were operationalised, and 5 new cognitive aide, checklist, or algorithm items were actioned. Of tested items, over 94% of respondents recommended their clinical use. Iterative changes were made to protocols, checklist and algorithm items following simulation testing.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over a 5-year period, this program has become embedded in routine clinical operations by demonstrating long-term feasibility and sustainability, high levels of participant satisfaction, and translational impact by focusing on quality assurance initiatives and interprofessional team training.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Frequency-tuned impedance matching for pulsed capacitively coupled plasmas: analysis of self-consistent circuit-plasma coupling
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Pulsed capacitively coupled plasmas (CCPs) exhibit strongly time-dependent electrical characteristics because the plasma density, sheath structure, and plasma conductivity change as a function of time within each pulse period. This makes impedance matching difficult when the driving frequency and matching-network elements are fixed. In this work, a self-consistent circuit-plasma simulation model is used to investigate frequency-tuned impedance matching for pulsed CCPs. The model couples an implicit PIC/MCC plasma kinetic simulation with an external RF circuit including a generator, matching network, and reactor stray branch. The plasma impedance is extracted from the simulated CCP voltage and current waveforms using Fourier analysis. Under fixed-frequency operation at
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>
                        
                      </jats:tex-math>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mn>13.56</mml:mn>
                          <mml:mtext> </mml:mtext>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mi>MHz</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , the reflection coefficient magnitude remains high during the effective pulse-on phase and a pronounced reflected-power peak appears after pulse ignition. A frequency-tuned matching strategy is then developed by determining, from the time-dependent plasma impedance, the driving frequency that minimizes the reflection coefficient magnitude while the matching-network elements remain fixed. The results show that frequency tuning strongly suppresses the reflected power during the pulse-on phase, while the power absorbed by the plasma changes only weakly under the imposed constant-generator-output-power condition. The results provide a proof-of-principle demonstration that driving-frequency modulation can compensate for transient impedance variations, reduce the reflected-power burden, and improve matching efficiency in pulsed CCPs without changing the matching-network elements within the pulse.
                  </jats:p>

title: Study of the ionization in air-breathing electric rockets with VLEO atmospheric propellants and typical laboratory mixtures
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This work investigates the ionization of atmospheric propellant in air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP) systems for satellites operating in Very-Low Earth Orbit (VLEO). Plasma formation inside the ionization chamber of an air-breathing thruster is studied to gain insights on physical phenomena involved in ABEP technology. A time-dependent zero-dimensional model of the plasma chamber is formulated, that accounts for a comprehensive set of reactions for nitrogen, oxygen and argon. This model is implemented within a numerical framework to simulate plasma ignition at different operating parameters defined to describe geometry, intake behaviour, input power, magnetic field interactions, acceleration mechanism, and VLEO environmental conditions. The simulation results include the evolution in time of plasma density, composition and reaction rates during the ignition transient until stationary conditions. The study identifies the plasma ignition envelope by analysing the dependencies of plasma properties on mass flow rate, electron temperature, and ions-to-neutrals residence times ratio. The composition and density of the plasma are characterized across different regimes, revealing a transition between molecular and atomic ions dominance. NO

Comparison between results on different mixtures are performed and approximation laws to facilitate experimental validation are derived, which can help improving the accuracy of plasma diagnostic measurements for experimental conditions relevant to ABEP testing. Furthermore, it is shown that the use of argon as substitute of atomic oxygen in low-density air-like mixture plasma does not provide representative results.

title:
Three-dimensional numerical simulation study on nanosecond CO
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    laser cleaning of particle contaminants on the surface of fused silica optical components
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Sputtered particulate contaminants during the laser damage process of fused silica optical components are one of the key factors causing laser damage to optical components. Nanosecond CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    laser cleaning is an effective method for removing fused silica particle contaminants from the surface of fused silica optical components. To explore the mechanism of CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    laser cleaning, this paper establishes a three-dimensional multiphysics coupling model of laser cleaning. Unlike previous laser cleaning studies where the contaminants and the substrate were different materials, this paper investigates the laser cleaning problem where the particles and the substrate are the same material. It points out that the strong absorption of laser by the material and the optical properties of the particles are key to their cleaning ability. The paper proposes two criteria for the desorption of fused silica particles: an inertial criterion and a contact stress criterion. In addition, other influencing factors, including pulse width, particle shape, and spacing between particles, are also discussed in this paper.
                  </jats:p>

title: Experimental tuning of electron energy gain via laser focus shift in a laser-driven plasma wakefield accelerator
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a combined experimental and simulation study on electron acceleration in a laser-driven plasma wakefield accelerator utilizing the plasma telescope mechanism. By employing a 15-J laser with its focal spot smaller than the matching condition, and systematically tuning the laser focus position relative to the gas cell entrance, we generate an electron beam with energy of up to 1.4 GeV when the laser is focused a few millimeters upstream of the plasma entrance. We further observe that electron self-injection and subsequent acceleration occur only when the laser is focused within 2.2 mm upstream to 2.4 mm downstream of the gas-cell entrance. Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations reproduce the experimental observations and predict a maximum electron energy of 2.2 GeV at the optimal focal position. Both the experiments and simulations reveal a clear injection threshold when the laser focus is placed too far upstream of the plasma entrance. In this case, excessive laser diffraction prevents efficient refocusing by the plasma telescope, thereby suppressing wakefield injection and acceleration. These results provide experimental evidence that the plasma telescope mechanism can support the generation of GeV-scale electron beams in laser wakefield accelerators. Furthermore, they identify the laser focal position on the plasma density up-ramp as a critical parameter governing electron injection and energy gain, offering important guidance for the optimization of future plasma-telescope-based acceleration schemes.</jats:p>

title: Nonlinear dynamics of dual acoustic waves in dusty plasmas on the lunar shady-side
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Weakly nonlinear electrostatic waves are examined in a dusty-plasma model for the lunar nightside wake during the Moon’s passage through the Earth’s magnetotail. The linear spectrum contains a fast dust-ion-acoustic wave (DIAW), governed mainly by ion inertia, and a slow dust-acoustic wave (DAW), governed by dust inertia. A Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) reduction shows that the DAW remains rarefactive over the considered electron-depletion and temperature-ratio ranges, whereas the DIAW crosses a polarity-reversal boundary, where the quadratic nonlinearity vanishes. This boundary marks the limit of the KdV ordering rather than a physical amplitude singularity. Retaining cubic nonlinearity gives a Gardner description of the near-critical DIAW. Within the adopted lunar-wake parameter domain, the critical line remains in the positive-cubic-coefficient region, so the model admits polarity-selective Gardner solitons and the dual-polarity modified Korteweg–de Vries (mKdV) limit but does not reach the flat-top Gardner limiting sequence. The results identify how the two acoustic branches differ in nonlinear polarity and in the accessibility of near-critical electrostatic structures in this lunar-wake model.</jats:p>

Resonant Excitation of the Boundary Distortion of a Cold Semi-Infinite Plasma by Electromagnetic Radiation
items.abstract: <jats:p>The effect of external electromagnetic radiation on the curvature of the boundary of a semi-infinite cold plasma, together with the parameters and properties of surface oscillations localized near this boundary, is considered. A new system of two equations has been derived from the known hydrodynamic description of cold electron plasma motion to analyze the nonlinear interaction of a strong electromagnetic field with an electrostatic wave at the plasma surface and with the cavity that appears at the plasma boundary. The self-consistent excitation of electrostatic waves and appearing cavities takes place under certain conditions and may be provided by special choices of initial-boundary magnitudes of perturbation parameters. The corresponding approximate description makes it possible to reveal basic peculiarities of perturbations under consideration and to identify methods of exciting such disturbances of a plasma boundary state. The investigated properties of the surface curvature can be used to obtain current information about the state of the plasma surface and for active influence on it by means, for example, of electromagnetic beams.</jats:p>

Mechanobiological and nutrigenomic regulation of mesenchymal stem cell fate: epigenetic and epitranscriptomic mechanisms in orthopedic regeneration
container-title: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
items.abstract: <jats:p>Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) are key regulators of musculoskeletal regeneration, since their differentiation into osteogenic, chondrogenic, adipogenic, and other stromal lineages governs tissue repair and remodeling. Growing evidence suggests that MSC fate is not determined solely by intrinsic developmental programs, but is continuously influenced by environmental cues, including mechanical loading, nutritional status, inflammation, oxidative stress, metabolic condition, and the tissue microenvironment. Exercise and dietary polyphenols constitute two biologically distinct environmental inputs that may potentially converge on partially overlapping regulatory networks. Mechanical stimulation triggers mechanotransduction networks involving Wnt/β-catenin, bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), YAP/TAZ, NF-κB, and related signaling routes, while polyphenols regulate redox homeostasis, inflammatory pathways, cellular metabolism, and transcriptional control. Although these pathways provide a plausible basis for convergence, direct experimental evidence demonstrating their coordinated action within MSCs remains limited. These signals also engage epigenetic processes, such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs, as well as emerging epitranscriptomic mechanisms, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification. Together, these regulatory strata form a dynamic interface through which environmental information can reshape MSC lineage commitment and regenerative capability. Recent experimental evidence further indicates that m6A-dependent mechanisms may be involved in osteogenic–angiogenic coupling and bone repair, whereas age-related epigenetic remodeling drives dysfunction in mesenchymal stem cells and biases their lineage commitment. Multi-omics approaches offer a way to link these molecular responses with metabolic, biomechanical, and clinical phenotypes, thereby facilitating the design of individualized regenerative strategies. This review puts forward a proposed mechanobiological–nutrigenomic framework in which exercise and polyphenol-derived signals may intersect with signaling, epigenetic, and epitranscriptomic networks to influence mesenchymal stem cell fate and musculoskeletal regeneration. Because most existing evidence assesses exercise, polyphenols, or discrete molecular pathways independently, the proposed convergence should be viewed as a conceptual and empirically testable framework rather than a well-established integrated mechanism. The framework also highlights key translational obstacles, including limited evidence from human studies, heterogeneity in polyphenol exposure, incomplete definition of exercise-responsive epitranscriptomic mechanisms, and the need for direct research examining combined interventions.</jats:p>

title: The Metabolism–Proteostasis Axis in Stem Cell Fate and Bone Marrow Niche Homeostasis: A Review
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The bone marrow niche is a dynamic microenvironment that maintains hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) by integrating biochemical, mechanical, metabolic, and inflammatory cues. Rather than acting as a passive structural compartment, the niche coordinates stem cell quiescence, self-renewal, and lineage commitment. Over the last decade, significant advances have revealed that cellular metabolism is not merely a consequence of stem cell activation but a central regulator of stem cell identity. Glycolysis, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid oxidation, and amino acid metabolism continuously adapt to environmental demands, while nutrient-sensing pathways such as AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) orchestrate metabolic remodeling according to cellular energetic status. Simultaneously, proteostasis has emerged as a fundamental determinant of stem cell function. Molecular chaperones (such as HSP70, HSP90, and BiP), the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and autophagy preserve protein quality, mitochondrial integrity, and stress adaptation. Crucially, metabolic activity and proteostasis are interconnected through reciprocal mechanisms involving ATP, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and mitochondrial dynamics. This integrated network influences not only HSCs but also mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) and endothelial cells within the niche. Consequently, disrupting metabolic or proteostatic homeostasis can contribute to stem cell dysfunction, aging, and hematological malignancies. In this narrative review, we discuss recent advances in metabolic regulation and proteostasis in HSCs and MSCs, emphasizing their functional integration. Together, these interconnected processes may contribute to the regulation of stem cell fate and bone marrow niche homeostasis, providing a conceptual framework for future studies and potential therapeutic applications.</jats:p>

title: Simulation und experimentelle Validierung der Wirkung von Schwemmholzverklausungen
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstrakt</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Während starkregeninduzierter Hochwasserereignisse kommt es häufig zur Mobilisierung von schwimmfähigem Treibgut, insbesondere von Holz. An Engstellen in Flussläufen kann sich das Treibgut verhängen und sukzessive dammartige Strukturen bilden, welche den Abflussquerschnitt teilweise oder vollständig blockieren. Diese als Verklausungen bekannten Strukturen treten häufig an Querbauwerken wie Brücken auf. Durch die Blockade des Fließquerschnitts entsteht ein Rückstau im Gewässer, welcher zusätzliche hydrostatische und hydrodynamische Belastungen verursacht, die zur Beschädigung und zum Einsturz des betroffenen Brückenbauwerks führen können. Mangels Berechnungsgrundlagen ist eine gesicherte Bemessung gegenüber Belastungen aus Hochwasserabfluss und Verklausung nicht möglich, wobei der Bedarf angesichts des Klimawandels und der daraus resultierenden intensiveren und höherfrequenten Hochwasserereignisse steigt. Im Beitrag werden Forschungsarbeiten des Forschungsbereichs Konstruktiver Ingenieurbau der HTW Dresden vorgestellt, in deren Rahmen ein Simulationsmodell für Schwemmholzverklausungen entwickelt wurde. Zur Kalibrierung und Validierung des Modells wurde ein Versuchsstand errichtet, an dem Untersuchungen an künstlich hergestellten Verklausungen durchgeführt wurden. Das nunmehr kalibrierte und validierte Simulationsmodell ermöglicht systematische numerische Untersuchungen, aus denen zukünftig Lastannahmen abgeleitet werden können.</jats:p>

An in situ atmospheric-pressure dielectric barrier discharge setup for time-resolved synchrotron characterisation of cerium metal-organic frameworks
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>In situ</jats:italic>
                    investigation of plasma–material interactions are essential for understanding material stability and transformation mechanisms under non-thermal plasma conditions. Nevertheless, such studies remain challenging due to the limited availability of plasma reactors compatible with synchrotron-based structural and spectroscopic techniques. Here, we present the design, construction, and characterisation of a dedicated
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    atmospheric-pressure dielectric barrier discharge reactor enabling quasi-simultaneous x-ray diffraction (XRD) and x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) during plasma exposure. The compact reactor integrates a quartz discharge tube, an exchangeable powder sample holder, a controlled gas-flow system, and aligned driven and grounded electrodes. The geometry ensures that the reactive gas stream passes directly through the sample while maintaining optical and x-ray access. Stable plasma operation is achieved at 20.8 kHz and peak-to-peak voltages up to 14 kV with various gas mixtures. Electrical diagnostics based on current–voltage measurements and Lissajous analysis quantify discharge power, transferred charge, and effective plasma capacitance, confirming reproducible and tuneable plasma conditions. Optical imaging and thermocouple measurements further validate discharge position in relation to the sample and provide temperature control up to 200 °C. Compatibility with synchrotron radiation investigation is demonstrated at a dedicated beamtime at ESRF (BM23) through time-resolved transmission XAS and XRD measurements. As a proof of concept, cerium-based metal–organic frameworks, Ce-CAU-41 and −44, were investigated, illustrating the capability of the setup to track plasma-induced structural and chemical changes in real time. The developed reactor provides a robust and flexible tool for
                    <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                    synchrotron studies of plasma-driven processes and enables mechanistic investigations of material transformations under atmospheric-pressure plasma conditions.
                  </jats:p>

title: Dust Generation During Milling of Grey Cast Iron: Parametric Modeling of Particle Size Distribution
items.abstract: <jats:p>Particle size distribution (PSD) of dust generated during machining is a key parameter for designing dust control systems. In this study, 90 dust samples were collected from two milling machines under three milling modes, with and without air supply, at five points in the working area. The study is limited to grey cast iron grade SCH20 and to the investigated milling conditions. Sieve analysis was used, with laser diffraction (LALLS) validation for ten samples. The dust showed high polydispersity: the calculated number-based mean particle size ranged from 16.6 to 228 µm. In the investigated conditions, samples collected with air supply showed a smaller median particle size (70–120 μm vs. 50–70 μm); however, because different machines, tools and cutting parameters were used, this is interpreted as an observed effect rather than an isolated causal factor of air cooling. Comparison of the methods showed agreement in mass representation (5–7% discrepancy). However, in number-based representation, LALLS detected up to 35% of particles below the sieve analysis lower limit (26 μm). Calculated number-based PSDs were approximated using Weibull and lognormal distributions. The lognormal model provided slightly higher statistical accuracy (RMSE 2.4 vs. 2.9). Nevertheless, within the investigated conditions, the Weibull distribution is a provisional modeling option as a conservative engineering approximation for practical tasks. Its extrapolation below 26 μm predicts a higher proportion of fine fractions than the lognormal model; however, direct measurements of PM10, PM2.5 and PM1 were not performed, and these estimates are preliminary and require validation. Parameterized PSD models are presented for each milling mode and sampling point.</jats:p>

title: Glucose-dependent Sch9p signaling disrupts spatial cell organization and leads to widespread cell death and reduced long-term survival in yeast colonies
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cell-cell coordination is essential for the development and maintenance of multicellular systems, including true multicellular organisms and spatially structured microbial communities. Disruption of cellular coordination and differentiation is detrimental and can be associated with pathological states, such as during mammalian tumorigenesis. It is now well established that colonies of single-cell microbial species, including baker’s yeast, become organized into differentiated subpopulations. However, the responsible molecular pathways remain poorly understood. Using a spatially differentiated yeast colony model composed of two major, metabolically distinct subpopulations, we investigated how environmental cues and signaling pathways regulate multicellular coordination and differentiation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Live-colony imaging, cell-specific staining, label-free proteomics, and genetic analyses were combined to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of colony differentiation and to identify key regulatory pathways controlling coordinated multicellular development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We demonstrate here that in the presence of high glucose, yeast colonies fail to mature into differentiated complex communities. A targeted genetic screen identified the conserved protein kinase Sch9, a functional homolog of mammalian Akt, as a major negative regulator of cellular coordination and differentiation in yeast colonies. In the presence of high glucose, Sch9p repressed the function of the transcriptional regulator Hap4, resulting in impaired respiration and disruption of coordinated colony development. Consequently, colonies failed to establish their characteristic spatial differentiation program, including localized metabolic reprogramming, interactions between specialized cell subpopulations, and spatially restricted cell death. Instead, distinct cell types were distributed irregularly throughout the colony and underwent widespread premature cell death, markedly reducing the long-term survival of the colony population. Disruption of the
                      <jats:italic>SCH9</jats:italic>
                      gene restored Hap4p-dependent respiration and coordinated colony development in high glucose, enabling the formation of spatially differentiated colonies and promoting their long-term viability.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings identify a glucose-responsive Sch9p–Hap4p signaling axis that regulates multicellular coordination and differentiation of yeast cells in colonies. We show that glucose-induced Sch9p signaling disrupts Hap4p-dependent cellular coordination and differentiation and promotes widespread cell death, thereby limiting the long-term survival of spatial yeast communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Non-Thermal Pretreatments for Hot-Air Drying of Whole Black Chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa): Comparison of Cold Plasma and Indirect Ultrasound
items.abstract: <jats:p>Whole black chokeberries, with their surface wax and firm structure, dry slowly. Atmospheric-pressure cold plasma for 150 or 300 s (CP2.5 and CP5) and indirect ultrasound for 30 min (IUS) were compared before hot-air drying of whole fruit at 50, 60 and 70 °C, with drying duration fixed within each temperature. CP2.5 gave the strongest kinetic response, reducing the time to a moisture ratio of 0.10 (t10) by 19–25%, against 12–17% for CP5 and 11–13% for IUS, and increasing the apparent effective moisture diffusivity by 24–34%. It also gave the lowest mean CIELAB browning index, 64–72% below the control, and the highest mean phenolic, flavonoid and anthocyanin contents among the hot-air-dried groups, with total flavonoid content significantly higher than the control at all temperatures; all remained below the freeze-dried reference. CP5 gave the lowest and IUS the highest shrinkage, and IUS did not differ from the control in composition or antioxidant capacity. Raising the temperature from 50 to 70 °C reduced control t10 by 59%; anthocyanin means were 8–15% lower at 70 °C than at 50 °C. The Arrhenius slopes of the four groups did not differ significantly. Extending plasma exposure reduced the kinetic benefit; the compositional advantage of CP2.5 over CP5 was not statistically demonstrated.</jats:p>

Mechanisms and improvement strategies for T-cell exhaustion in bispecific T-cell engager therapy: a review
items.abstract:
<jats:p>Bispecific T-cell engagers (TCEs), which redirect endogenous T cells to eliminate tumor cells through dual targeting of CD3 and tumor-associated antigens (TAAs), have achieved remarkable success in hematological malignancies. However, T-cell exhaustion driven by persistent antigen stimulation has increasingly become a major mechanism underlying treatment resistance and relapse, characterized by loss of effector functions, upregulation of inhibitory receptors, and transcriptional–epigenetic reprogramming—a process potentially amplified by supraphysiological, non-physiological CD3 crosslinking, a model derived primarily from preclinical data. This narrative review outlines the molecular features and clinical landscape of both classical BiTEs and IgG-like TCEs and provides an in-depth analysis of the characteristics and mechanisms of TCE-related T-cell exhaustion, with special emphasis on transcription factor networks, synergistic inhibitory receptor signaling, and metabolic–epigenetic alterations. We evaluate improvement strategies using an evidence-level stratification approach and interpret their translational prospects based on key trial data including LimiTec, MajesTEC-3, and EPCORE FL-1. We distinguish treatment-free intervals (TFIs) from fixed-duration regimens and discuss their differential applicability across hematological malignancies; in multiple myeloma (MM), we explicitly distinguish T-cell exhaustion–driven cellular immunosuppression from humoral immunodeficiency secondary to plasma-cell depletion, which require distinct mitigation strategies. As a narrative (non-systematic) review, evidence is appraised with explicit study-type labels; many proposed strategies remain preclinical or early-phase, and none has yet been validated in randomized trials. This review aims to provide a reference for overcoming TCE resistance and sustaining durable T-cell antitumor capacity.</jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evidence retrieval and appraisal. This is a narrative (non-systematic) review. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and major congress abstract archives (American Society of Hematology, American Society of Clinical Oncology, European Hematology Association) through August 2026 using combinations of the terms “bispecific T-cell engager”, “BiTE”, “T-cell exhaustion”, “treatment-free interval”, “fixed-duration”, and agent-specific names. Peer-reviewed full publications were prioritized; conference abstracts are explicitly identified and interpreted as preliminary. Where evidence derives from chronic infection, solid-tumor, or CAR-T models rather than TCE-treated patients, this is stated in the text. The Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) levels are used as an approximate orientation only and are complemented throughout by an explicit study-type label (preclinical, early-phase clinical, single-arm prospective, randomized, retrospective). No formal systematic screening, risk-of-bias assessment, or meta-analysis was performed, and citation selection reflects the authors’ expert judgment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Oxygen modulation as a factor to improve the generation of functional stem cell-derived pancreatic beta cells
container-title: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Stem cell-derived pancreatic beta (SC-β) cells are a promising therapeutic approach to replace lost pancreatic beta cells and restore blood glucose regulation in individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D). The use of SC-β cells as a research tool and clinical therapy is limited by various deficits of current SC-β cells compared to endogenous adult pancreatic beta cells. The effects of oxygen during
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      SC-β cell differentiation have been understudied despite the ability of oxygen to act as a developmental signal, influence stem cell regulation, and affect the differentiation capacity of stem cells for development into specific cell lineages.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We performed stem cell culture and SC-β cell differentiations in a 3D culture system in oxygen-controlled incubators. We developed a Low Oxygen Protocol that exposes embryonic stem (ES) cells to a 5% incubator oxygen environment before performing the SC-β cell differentiation stages at ambient incubator oxygen conditions (∼18–20%). For comparison, all Low Oxygen SC-β cell replicates were paired with Control SC-β cells that were only cultured in ambient oxygen conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Low Oxygen Protocol generates SC-β cells with enhanced glucose-stimulated insulin secretory function compared to Control SC-β cells. ES cells respond to low oxygen conditions with increased HIF-1α protein accumulation and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism. While the Low Oxygen Protocol did not affect transcriptional characteristics of beta cell maturity, the Low Oxygen SC-β cells had a more aerobic metabolic phenotype with increased mitochondrial respiratory parameters. The functional improvement of the Low Oxygen SC-β cells persisted after transplantation into a diabetic mouse model, where mice with Low Oxygen SC-β cell grafts had a significant, acute reduction of hyperglycemia compared to mice with Control SC-β cell grafts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In this study, we identified a Low Oxygen SC-β cell differentiation protocol that generates SC-β cells with improved functional and metabolic characteristics compared to Control SC-β cells. Utilizing oxygen as a developmental factor during
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      SC-β cell differentiations is a promising approach to address some SC-β cell deficits and may generate high-quality cells for use in research and as a cell therapy for T1D.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Resonant Excitation of the Boundary Distortion of a Cold Semi-Infinite Plasma by Electromagnetic Radiation
items.abstract: <jats:p>The effect of external electromagnetic radiation on the curvature of the boundary of a semi-infinite cold plasma, together with the parameters and properties of surface oscillations localized near this boundary, is considered. A new system of two equations has been derived from the known hydrodynamic description of cold electron plasma motion to analyze the nonlinear interaction of a strong electromagnetic field with an electrostatic wave at the plasma surface and with the cavity that appears at the plasma boundary. The self-consistent excitation of electrostatic waves and appearing cavities takes place under certain conditions and may be provided by special choices of initial-boundary magnitudes of perturbation parameters. The corresponding approximate description makes it possible to reveal basic peculiarities of perturbations under consideration and to identify methods of exciting such disturbances of a plasma boundary state. The investigated properties of the surface curvature can be used to obtain current information about the state of the plasma surface and for active influence on it by means, for example, of electromagnetic beams.</jats:p>

title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning Framework with the Quadratic Stark Effect for Predicting Red Fluorescent Protein Absorption Band Maxima
items.abstract: <jats:p>We developed a machine learning workflow using descriptors from ground-state quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories to predict the absorption maxima of red fluorescent proteins with the DsRed-type chromophore. Our analysis is based on a dataset consisting of 1600 entries from QM/MM MD frames extracted from model systems of four fluorescent proteins. The workflow enables the prediction of the dipole moment variation upon excitation (DMV) from the chromophore geometry and protein environment descriptors. The chromophore geometry, hydrogen bonds, electrostatic potentials, and π-stacking interactions were used in an ensemble of support vector regression (SVR) and LightGBM models. The loss function consisted of the frame-wise DMV mean absolute error (MAE) and the Wasserstein distance between the reference and predicted distributions of the DMV. Of the tested approaches, the median DMV values from state-averaged complete active space self-consistent field (sa-CASSCF(4/4)) calculations gave the best quadratic Stark fit. Leave-one-protein-out cross-validation resulted in a mean protein-wise MAE of 0.370 a.u. and a mean Wasserstein distance of 0.197 a.u. The test set contained three proteins; the predicted absorption maxima had an MAE of 0.02 eV relative to the experiment, with all individual errors below 0.05 eV even for the FusionRed protein, which is genetically distant from the training set. This indicates that accounting for the distant amino acids by their contributions to electrostatic potentials is a proper technique. Permutation analysis identified bond lengths as the most influential descriptors, which were followed by hydrogen bonding and electrostatic potentials. These results support trajectory-based machine learning for spectral prediction.</jats:p>

title: Implementation of Machine Learning Algorithms Using Scala
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
items.abstract:
<jats:p>Machine learning is an important part of modern technology because it enables computers to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without requiring instructions for every situation. Today, it is used in various fields, including healthcare, banking, education, business analysis, and recommendation systems. As the amount of data continues to increase, choosing the right algorithm, programming language, and development tools has become an important part of building effective machine learning applications.
This research paper focuses on implementing five commonly used machine learning algorithms using Scala: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and K-Means Clustering. Scala is a programming language that combines object-oriented and functional programming features and runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Its compatibility with Apache Spark makes it a useful option for developing applications that involve data processing and, where required, distributed computing.
The paper discusses how these algorithms work, how they can be implemented using Scala-based tools, and how their performance can be evaluated. It also examines the advantages and challenges of using Scala and Apache Spark for machine learning. Suitable evaluation measures are considered for regression, classification, and clustering tasks. The experimental results are intended to be collected from actual model implementations so that the comparison is based on observed performance rather than assumptions. Overall, the study aims to provide a clear understanding of these algorithms and the factors that influence their suitability for different machine learning problems.</jats:p>

title: A Compositional Inverse Model for Reconstructing Complete Grain‐Size Distributions From X‐Ray Fluorescence Core‐Scanning Spectra
container-title: Journal of Geophysical Research: Machine Learning and Computation
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The analysis of particulate sediments faces a resolution divide. Geochemical variations are increasingly scanned non‐destructively at sub‐millimeter resolution by means of X‐ray fluorescence core scanning (XRF‐CS). Yet, key physical properties such as particle‐size distributions remain labor‐intensive, costly, and destructive to measure. Full XRF‐CS spectra, however, contain more information than extracted elemental intensities alone because they reflect broader high‐energy photon interactions with particulate sediment. Here, we address this divide by formulating the reconstruction of complete grain‐size distributions from full XRF‐CS spectra as a compositional inverse problem. Our approach combines compositional data treatment, reduced‐rank representations of both XRF‐CS and grain‐size data, and Partial Least Squares regression in latent space. The model learns a low‐dimensional mapping between spectral variation and distributional grain‐size structure, allowing complete grain‐size distributions to be reconstructed at core‐scanner resolution from a limited set of reference samples. We evaluate the framework using a demanding single‐core benchmark spanning fine background sedimentation and diverse coarse‐grained event layers, while its calibration‐based design makes it applicable to other settings where grain‐size variability is expressed in XRF‐CS spectra. Rigorous validation against independent measurements at multiple spatial scales shows that reconstructed quantiles and moments robustly reproduce the measured grain‐size structure. Performance is strongest in fine‐grained intervals and deteriorates when scanning resolution approaches the prevailing grain size, indicating a practical scale limit. By extending XRF‐CS from scalar geochemical proxies toward distribution‐level physical‐property reconstruction, the framework opens new opportunities for automated event‐layer detection and frequency analysis in natural‐hazard studies, as well as high‐resolution climate reconstructions from sedimentary archives.</jats:p>

title: Daily Reservoir Storage Ratio Prediction Using Machine Learning: Germeçtepe Dam, Türkiye
items.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate daily reservoir storage estimates support water management and irrigation planning. This study compared seven models—linear regression, decision tree, random forest, XGBoost, recurrent neural network, gated recurrent unit, and long short-term memory—for estimating the reservoir storage ratio (RSR) of Germeçtepe Dam, Türkiye. Daily observations from 2008–2025 were evaluated using a chronological training–test split, with previous-day RSR and observed target-day meteorological variables as predictors. XGBoost achieved the lowest test RMSE (0.65%), followed by RF (0.66%), with both attaining R2 = 0.9994. RNN, GRU, and LSTM yielded RMSE values of 0.82%, 0.88%, and 1.23%, respectively. Compared with persistence (RMSE = 0.78%), XGBoost and RF reduced RMSE by approximately 16.2% and 15.2%, respectively. Permutation feature importance identified previous-day RSR as the dominant predictor in both ensemble models. Errors generally increased at higher storage levels for both the conventional models and the persistence baseline, with RF outperforming persistence under high-storage conditions. These findings demonstrate that relatively simple models can outperform recurrent architectures in this setting. Because target-day meteorological observations were used, operational one-day-ahead forecasting requires validation with meteorological forecasts.</jats:p>

title:
Characterisation, simulation and optimisation of a gridless LaB
                    <sub>6</sub>
                    hollow cathode DC plasma source for plasma ion-assisted electron beam deposition of optical coatings
container-title: Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The Plasma Deposition Source (PDS) is a gridless source for plasma ion-assisted deposition (PIAD) of electron beam evaporated optical coatings. PDS geometry, electrical and water-cooling feedthroughs provide a retrofittable configuration to most vacuum deposition chambers. The PDS utilises an inductively heated (100 kHz) LaB
                    <jats:sub>6</jats:sub>
                    hot hollow cathode, providing large-surface-area thermionic emission of a DC glow discharge at low vacuum pressure in the deposition chamber (typically 2 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−4</jats:sup>
                    mbar). The PDS incorporates a pressure differential between axially separated cathode and anode regions, with typical pressures of 2 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−3</jats:sup>
                    mbar and 2 × 10
                    <jats:sup>−4</jats:sup>
                    mbar, respectively, providing enhanced LaB
                    <jats:sub>6</jats:sub>
                    hollow cathode performance, self-sustaining plasma operation and reduced substrate heat loading and particulate contamination from the cathode. Retarding field energy analyser and Langmuir probe plasma diagnostic measurements and Monte Carlo simulation are described and used to characterise and optimise plasma output and establish fundamental understanding of PDS operation. The PDS provides an optimal ion energy range (5–50 eV) and enhanced ion current density (ICD; ∼0.4 mA cm
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    at 90 cm distance from the PDS to substrates) suitable for PIAD of densified amorphous optical thin films. Controllable PIAD over an extended deposition area is achieved using a tuneable magnetic field provided by a solenoid formed axially on the exterior of the anode assembly. Automated PDS control is described, providing stable output of plasma ion energy and current density. PIAD of densified single TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and SiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    layers (typical deposition rates of 0.6 and 0.7 nm s
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , respectively) is demonstrated as a function of PDS parameters and plasma ion adatom arrival rate. The influence of the impinging plasma ions is shown to be a thresholding process, where a minimum ICD is required to achieve film densification with a typical ion-to-deposited adatom ratio of ⩾1.2. PIAD of an 11-layer TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    /SiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    multilayer notch filter with no spectral drift over an extended substrate deposition area is also demonstrated.
                  </jats:p>

title: A Machine Learning - Based Framework for Acoustic Snoring Classification
items.abstract:
<jats:p>Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) remains
significantly underdiagnosed due to the high cost and
limited availability of standard polysomnography. This
study presents a machine learning framework for
acoustic snoring classification using synchronized
ambient and tracheal audio recordings from the
Polysomnography Audio (PSG-Audio) dataset,
comprising 192 subjects and 81,408 ten-second
segments. Comprehensive feature extraction was
performed to capture spectral, temporal, and harmonic
characteristics of snoring sounds, including Melfrequency cepstral coefficients, spectral features,
temporal features, and chroma descriptors. Four
supervised classifiers - Random Forest, Gradient
Boosting, Support Vector Machine, and Multi-Layer
Perceptron (MLP) - were systematically evaluated. The
MLP classifier achieved the best performance with
94.38% accuracy, 93.9% sensitivity, and an Area Under
the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUCROC) of 0.9855. These findings demonstrate that
feature-based acoustic modeling, combined with neural
network architecture, can provide reliable and noninvasive snoring classification for potential OSA
screening applications. The proposed framework offers
a scalable solution for integration into intelligent sleep
monitoring systems, reducing reliance on resourceintensive polysomnography.</jats:p>

title: Causal discovery guided machine learning framework for optimizing sustainable concrete mix design using GGBS and microsilica
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The use of supplementary cementitious materials such as Ground Granulated Blast Furnace Slag (GGBS) and microsilica provides a proven route to lowering the Portland cement content of structural concrete while improving its long-term mechanical performance. Predicting the resulting compressive, flexural, and split tensile strengths across a wide range of mix proportions and curing ages remains challenging, particularly when the directional relationships among mix variables are not made explicit. This study proposes a three-stage framework combining constraint-based causal structure learning, machine learning prediction, and mix design optimisation. A structured dataset of 285 observations was compiled from a laboratory programme covering three concrete grades (M25, M30, M35), five curing ages (7, 14, 28, 56, and 90 days), ten GGBS replacement levels (0 to 50%), and two microsilica conditions (0% and 5%). The Peter-Clark (PC) algorithm was applied to the observational data to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representing statistically inferred direct dependencies, interpreted in the light of established cement chemistry, among the input features and the three target properties. Three machine learning models (Random Forest, RF; Extreme Gradient Boosting, XGBoost; and a Multi-Layer Perceptron Artificial Neural Network, ANN) were trained on 80% of the data (228 samples) and evaluated on the remaining 20% (57 samples). XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy, with test-set R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    of 0.9921, 0.9925, and 0.9871 for CS, FS, and STS, and RMSE of 0.86, 0.05, and 0.02 MPa. The robustness of these results was confirmed by 50 repeated random splits (XGBoost CS R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                     = 0.9906 ± 0.0033) and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and the ML framework was benchmarked against linear, ridge, polynomial, and support vector regression. SHAP analysis identified curing age and concrete grade as the most influential predictors. The XGBoost prediction surface indicated GGBS replacements of 40 to 50% with 5% microsilica as the optimal configuration, delivering CS of 47 to 53 MPa at 90-day curing for M30 grade (a 22 to 37% improvement over the 28-day conventional reference) while reducing Portland cement content by approximately 45%. The framework provides an interpretable and reproducible tool for data-driven sustainable concrete mix design.
                  </jats:p>

title: Developing A Refined View of High Seas Pacific Salmon Distributions Through Machine Learning
items.abstract: <jats:p>The oceanic habitat conditions that Pacific salmon encounter during the pelagic life stage have a substantial effect on their distribution, growth, and survival. Fisheries and monitoring data collected in coastal marine and freshwater areas are often linked to conditions in oceanic habitat to attempt to explain patterns in salmon population productivity as their marine rearing habitats continue to change (Connors et al. 2020; Kitada et al. 2025; Ohlberger et al. 2025). However, a substantial source of uncertainty in such analyses stems from knowledge gaps regarding the habitats that salmon utilize while at sea. For this reason, many research efforts have worked to characterize the oceanic ranges of each species and how they relate to environmental factors like sea surface temperature (e.g., Abdul-Aziz et al. 2011; Langan et al. 2024; Alabia et al. 2025). Yet, these characterizations often present a coarse view of salmon distributions generated through summarizing or smoothing catch data over large spatial scales. In order to address contemporary challenges to salmon management, such as evaluating if and where/when high seas competition among species may take place (Ruggerone et al. 2023) or enhancing the effectiveness of enforcement activities against Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (IUU) fishing, new approaches are needed to maximize the spatiotemporal insight gained from composite historical datasets.</jats:p>

title: On-detector machine learning for beam-induced background rejection at a 10 TeV Muon collider
items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A 10 TeV Muon Collider is a compelling candidate for a future energy-frontier facility, offering unprecedented opportunities to explore the fundamental laws of particle physics. Muon decays in the collider ring produce intense beam-induced background (BIB) that can overwhelm detector occupancy and exceed readout bandwidth constraints. We investigate the potential of on-detector Machine Learning for BIB rejection in the vertex detector, exploiting pixel cluster shapes to distinguish background from collision products. We study three classes of lightweight neural-network architectures, and evaluate the feasibility of their implementation in hardware with high-level synthesis. Selected architectures achieve 88%–90% data reduction at 99% signal efficiency while requiring hardware resources compatible with potential ASIC implementation. These results demonstrate the potential of performing substantial BIB rejection directly in the pixel readout, providing a path towards meeting the tracker readout requirements at a future Muon Collider.</jats:p>
